content.text:
Here's what I've got so far (opencode's deep dive is still running in the background).

**Prodma** — Turkish manufacturing ERP, .NET Framework 4.6.1, WinForms + DevExpress, SQL Server.

| | |
|---|---|
| Product source | ~4,900 `.cs` files (the 678 `DevExpress.*` ones are decompiled reference assemblies, not yours) |
| Total LOC | 1.63M, of which **~411k (25%) is duplicate/backup files** |
| Schema | **422 entities, 1,175 FK associations** (`PrdomaModel.csdl`, Oct 2020) |
| Data access | 3 generations stacked: raw `SqlCommand` (~200 files, ~490 inline SQL strings), an EF EDMX model, and typed DataSets. Only 3 stored procs. |
| Modules | Satis, Muhasebe, Mrp, Raporlar, Servisler, Sistem, WebApi, WebPaylasim, ZamanliIslemler, Guncelleme |

Domain families by table count: `CARI` 52 (accounts/customers), `STOK` 32 (inventory), `MUHASEBE` 30 (accounting), `URETIM` 20 (production), `SERVIS` 11, `FATURA` 11, `KARGO` 10, `FIYAT` 10 (pricing), `SIPARIS` 9, `TEKLIF` 7, `CEK` 7, `RECETE` 6 (BOM), `KALIP` 5 (molds), plus IHRACAT/ITHALAT, PARTI (lot traceability), PLAKA. That profile reads as a **discrete manufacturer with import/export and batch traceability** — not a generic ERP.

Two things I want to flag before we go further:

**The codebase was versioned by filename, not git.** There are 134 date-suffixed files and 23 `Copy of…` files. `ListeYap.cs` ("make list") exists as ~15 dated copies of 11k–25k lines each — `ListeYap24032021.cs`, `ListeYap_150321.cs`, `ListeYap_080321.cs`… Nobody can tell you which one is live without running it. That's the single biggest risk to any port.

**Lobu is not an ERP framework.** It's an agent platform — connectors, feeds, an append-only `events` table, Behaviors, MCP. An ERP needs a transactional ledger, document-number sequences, and locking; Lobu's event store is append-only and explicitly forbids aggregating history on read paths, which is what ERP reporting *is*. So "port" can mean several very different projects, and which one you mean changes everything.

questions.question: When you say "port it to Lobu" — which of these is actually the goal?

options.label: Lobu on top, Prodma stays
options.description: Build a Prodma connector: sync CARI/STOK/FATURA/SIPARIS into Lobu as events, expose write actions. The ERP keeps running as the system of record; Lobu becomes the agent/automation/insight layer over it.

options.label: Replace the automation slice only
options.description: Kill ZamanliIslemler (scheduled jobs) and the ListeYap report/list generators, reimplement them as Lobu Behaviors. The ERP core (ledger, invoicing, stock) stays in .NET.

options.label: Rebuild the ERP itself on Lobu
options.description: Lobu becomes the backbone and Prodma is retired. Biggest scope — and where the append-only-events vs. transactional-ledger mismatch bites hardest.

options.label: Salvage the domain model
options.description: You mainly want the 422-entity schema and the hard business rules extracted into something modern; Lobu is one candidate host among others, not a settled decision.

questions.question: What's the current status of this system in the real world?

options.label: Live in production now
options.description: Real users depend on it daily. Any port is a migration with cutover risk and data continuity requirements.

options.label: Live but being wound down
options.description: Still running, but the plan is to replace it. Migration matters, but you can afford a parallel-run period.

options.label: Dormant / archived
options.description: Nobody is using it. This is a salvage job — extract value from the code and schema, no cutover pressure.

options.label: Never fully shipped
options.description: It was built but didn't reach real production use at scale.

questions.question: Do you have the SQL Server database, or only this source dump?

options.label: Full production DB with data
options.description: Best case — I can read the real schema, row counts, and which tables are actually used, which settles what's dead code far faster than reading 1.6M LOC.

options.label: Schema only, no data
options.description: I can get structure but not usage. Dead-vs-live table detection gets much harder.

options.label: Only this source folder
options.description: No DB at all. The EDMX model is the only schema evidence, and I can't tell live tables from abandoned ones.

options.label: Not sure / need to check
options.description: You'd have to go find out whether a backup or a live server still exists.

questions.question: What's driving this? Which pain do you most want gone?

options.label: Can't change it anymore
options.description: The codebase is unmaintainable — god files, duplicated copies, no one can safely make a change.

options.label: Windows-desktop-only
options.description: WinForms means no web, no mobile, no remote access. You want it usable outside the office.

options.label: Manual work that should be automated
options.description: People do repetitive things by hand that an agent could do — the classic Lobu use case.

options.label: Reporting / visibility
options.description: Getting answers out of the data is slow or impossible; the ListeYap report machinery is the bottleneck.

Schema is fully recoverable, and it's bigger than the 2020 model: **`ProdmaModel.Context.cs` (regenerated 22 Jun 2026) has 503 DbSets.** Entity classes are per-file (`CARI.cs` etc.).

One number worth sitting with: **`CARI` — the customer/account entity — has 153 scalar columns and 169 navigation properties.** That single table is the whole argument about what 20 years of ERP accretion looks like.

Now, the honest tension for a PoC. "Lobu replaces Prodma from scratch" can be demoed two very different ways, and only one of them survives contact with someone who knows ERP:

- **Build a small ERP on Lobu.** Show CRUD screens for customers, orders, invoices. The risk: an ERP-literate audience asks about double-entry posting, document-number sequences under concurrency, period close, KDV edge cases — and Lobu's append-only event store plus its "no aggregation on read paths" rule means you're either faking those or fighting the platform. A shallow ERP clone is the easiest demo to build and the easiest to dismiss.
- **Show the thing Prodma structurally cannot do.** Same domain, same seed data, but the demo is agents watching the business and acting — an overdue-receivable chase that reads CARI aging and drafts the dunning email, a stock-out that traces RECETE to a purchase order, a natural-language question that would have needed a new `ListeYap` file and three weeks. This plays to what Lobu actually is, and reframes "replace" as "obsolete the reason you needed 153 columns."

My recommendation is the second, with just enough of the first to make it concrete — but it depends entirely on who's watching.

content.text:
Both audits still running. Meanwhile, one correction that changes the picture.

I led with the append-only-events vs. transactional-ledger objection. **At under 20 concurrent users, that objection is much weaker than I made it sound.** Gapless invoice numbering, stock-movement contention, multi-replica coordination — these are hard at scale and nearly free at 20 users; a Postgres sequence plus an advisory lock covers it. Lobu's "no aggregation on read paths" rule is a codebase policy protecting against unbounded history growth, and 20 years of ERP data for a shop this size is millions of rows, not billions. So I'd no longer call that the fatal gap.

What moves to the top instead, now that compliance is non-negotiable:

1. **Turkish statutory compliance.** e-Fatura/e-Arşiv (GİB integration, mandatory), KDV declarations, BA/BS forms, Tekdüzen Hesap Planı. Lobu has none of this and it isn't a "we'll add a table" gap — e-Fatura means certified integrator contracts, XML envelopes, and legal retention. This is the one that can sink the whole claim, and it's the first thing Prodma's owner will ask about.
2. **Field-level authorization** — `YETKI_ALANLAR` already does this in Prodma. My strong prior is Lobu is org-scoped only.
3. **Schema-driven generic UI** — whether Owletto can render an arbitrary user-defined entity as a grid and a form, or whether every screen is hand-built React. If it's hand-built, "503 entities" becomes 503 screens of work and the PoC math collapses.
4. **Ad-hoc reporting without a code change** — Prodma's users get this today via the (awful) `ListeYap` machinery and DevExpress pivot grids.
5. **Document generation** — invoices and dispatch notes must print. That's DevExpress XtraReports today.

The audits will confirm or kill each of these with real evidence rather than my priors.

Let me save the interview outcome so it survives this session.

- **Use-case inventory is a DB table, not code.** `M_MENU` / `M_MENU_KULLANICI` / `M_MENU_BOLGE` / `M_MENU_SIRA` / `M_MENU_TIP` — menu is data-driven per-user and per-region; forms launch dynamically by name (`Type.GetType()` + `Activator.CreateInstance`, 166 call sites). `SELECT * FROM M_MENU` is worth more than reading 1.6M LOC. NOT yet obtained.

**Interview outcome (what the user actually wants):**
- Goal = **rebuild ERP on Lobu from scratch**, but the real point is a **gap analysis: "see where Lobu lacks"**. Not a migration — prod Prodma stays.
- Audience = **Prodma's owner** (domain expert, real prospect). Honesty beats polish.
- Scale = **under ~20 concurrent users**.

- Owner is sending Excel samples of the schema/data; seed data obtainable.

**Correction to my first take:** I led with "append-only `events` vs transactional ledger" as the fatal mismatch. **At <20 users that objection is weak** — gapless numbering and stock contention are nearly free at that scale (sequence + advisory lock). Lobu's no-aggregation-on-read-paths rule is a policy against unbounded history, and this dataset is millions of rows, not billions. # Shared brief — Prodma ERP → Lobu gap analysis

## Context
"Prodma" is a Turkish manufacturing ERP: .NET Framework 4.6.1, WinForms + DevExpress, SQL Server.
Source dump: `/Users/burakemre/Downloads/emre_project` — ~5,800 .cs files FLATTENED into one directory, no subfolders, no .sln, not a git repo.

**Goal of the overall project:** decide whether "Lobu" (a modern agent platform) could replace Prodma, and produce an HONEST list of where Lobu falls short. A wrong "this is easy" is far worse than "this is hard". The audience is Prodma's own owner, a domain expert who will catch hand-waving.

**Deployment reality:** under 20 concurrent users. So raw scale/throughput is NOT a concern. Correctness, domain completeness, and statutory compliance ARE.

## Navigating the flat codebase
- IGNORE any file whose `namespace` starts with `DevExpress` — decompiled third-party assemblies (678 files), not product code.
- Product namespaces: `Prodma.*`, `Satis`, `Listeler`, `AlisSatis`, `Muhasebe`, `Mrp`, `Ortak`, `Siparis`, `Mahsup`, `Teklif`, `Cek`, `AmbarFisleri`.
- **25% of the codebase is dead duplicates.** The team versioned by FILENAME, not git. Skip files matching: `*_[0-9]{6,8}.cs` (date suffixes like `_080321`, `24032021`), `Copy of *`, `*eski*` (eski = old), `*Yedek*` (yedek = backup). ~15 dated copies of `ListeYap*.cs` alone (11k–25k lines each). When several versions exist, read the one with NO date suffix.
- Naming convention: `XxxService.cs` (419 of them), `XxxCntrl.cs` (362, controllers), `XxxVm.cs` (706, view models), `XxxEn.cs` (373, enums), `Xxx.Designer.cs` (WinForms layout — SKIP, it's generated).
- Schema: `ProdmaModel.Context.cs` = live EF DbContext, **503 DbSets**. Entity classes are per-file, e.g. `CARI.cs` (153 scalar columns + 169 navigation properties). `PrdomaModel.csdl` (1.7MB) has full property/association definitions. `ProdmaModel.cs` is a 436-byte stub — NOT the schema.
- Data access is 3 generations stacked: raw ADO.NET `SqlCommand` (~200 files, ~490 inline SQL strings), the EF model, and typed DataSets. Only 3 stored procedures.

## The menu = the use-case inventory
`menu-tree.txt` (this directory) is the real `M_MENU` table from a live install: 11 top-level modules, 532 entries, 441 distinct screens. Lines marked `•` are screens with a form class in `[brackets]`; `▸` lines are folders. input.content:
---
name: reference_opencode_rejects_paths_outside_cwd
description: opencode CLI auto-rejects reads/writes outside its working directory, exits 0 anyway — stage inputs and outputs INSIDE the repo and use relative paths
metadata:
  type: reference
---

`opencode run` sandboxes file access to its working directory. Any absolute path outside it triggers
`permission requested: external_directory (...); auto-rejecting` and the tool call fails.

**The trap: the process still exits 0.** A fan-out of agents can report `exit=0` for every one while
every report file is MISSING and no work was done. Verified 2026-08-13 — a 4-agent wave "succeeded"
with zero output because the brief and the report paths were both in the session scratchpad.

**Fix:** stage the brief, reference data, and report destination INSIDE the target repo
(e.g. `_analysis/`), and tell the agent explicitly: "use ONLY relative paths inside your working
directory; absolute paths outside it are rejected." For the lobu repo this must be a
`make task-setup` worktree, never the main checkout (see AGENTS.md hard invariant).

**Always smoke-test before a wave:** one cheap `opencode run` that reads a staged file and writes a
sentinel, then `cat` the sentinel. Costs ~30s and catches a total wave failure.

Assert on the artifact (`[ -f report.md ] && wc -l`), never on the exit code.
Default model is `deepseek-v4-flash`. `--dir` sets the working directory.

Related: [[feedback_piped_make_exit_code_is_a_false_green]], [[project_prodma_erp_to_lobu_poc]]

result.output:
1	# UI surface audit — `packages/owletto`
2	
3	**One-line answer.** Lobu's UI is NOT "441 screens = 441 hand-built React files". There is a real, working schema-driven renderer: a JSON-Schema stored per user-defined entity type drives the list (table/board/gallery), the detail page, and the edit form for free. What is missing is the ERP **depth** of that renderer: the form and grid are flat-scalar only, and none of the transactional ergonomics (keyboard grid entry, master-detail lines, lookups, saved views, per-field filters, unsaved guards) or document outputs (PDF/Excel) exist. Feasible in kind; HARD in completeness.
4	
5	Scope caveat: I read real code + the `entity_types`/`entities` schema evidence on the server side only where it proves what the frontend renders. Everything cited is in `packages/owletto` unless marked `(server)`.
6	
7	---
8	
9	## 1. What the frontend actually renders — route map
10	
11	File-based routing (TanStack Router); all routes in `src/routeTree.gen.ts`, route files under `src/app/` (61 route `.tsx` files).
12	
13	- Public/auth: `/` landing, `/auth/*` (login, callback, accept-invitation, reset-password), `/oauth/*`, `/orgs/new`, `/slack/claim` — `src/app/auth/login.tsx`, `src/app/index.tsx`.
14	- Workspace shell `/$owner` (`src/app/$owner.tsx`) with static nav sections, `src/lib/owner-sections.ts:28`: Activity, Connectors, Agents, Behaviors, Memory, Settings.
15	- Bespoke product screens (hand-built): `/$owner/connectors/*`, `/$owner/agents/*` (incl. guardrails/skills/permissions/identity/models), `/$owner/behaviors/*`, `/$owner/events`, `/$owner/settings/organization`, `/$owner/entity-types/$slug` (type admin), deployments, members.
16	- **Schema-driven screens:** `/$owner/memory` hub (`src/app/$owner/memory/*`), the first-class type list `/$owner/<type>` (`src/app/$owner/$entityType/index.tsx:12`), and entity detail `/$owner/<type>/<slug>` resolved through the catch-all `/$owner/$` (`src/app/$owner/$.tsx:45`).
17	
18	So the UI is two populations: ~10 hand-built Lobu-product sections, and one generic "Memory" surface that renders *any* entity type.
19	
20	## 2. Generic, schema-driven components — the decisive question
21	
22	**YES.** An entity type carries a `metadata_schema` (JSON-Schema); the UI renders it generically end-to-end.
23	
24	- **List/grid** — `EntityTypeListPanel` (`src/components/entities/entity-type-list-panel.tsx:80`) feeds `EntityTableView` (`src/components/entities/entity-table-view.tsx:173`). Columns are *derived from the schema*: each `properties[k]` with `"x-table-column": true` becomes a sortable column (`entity-table-view.tsx:215-309`), formatted by annotation (`x-currency`, `format: date|uri`, `enum`, `x-link-entity-type` cross-links, `x-table-label`) via `resolveColumnFormat` (`entity-table-view.tsx:123`). Also derives parent/relationship/derived-measure columns (`entity-table-view.tsx:355-521`).
25	- **Alternate list views** — board (Kanban, drag-to-update) `src/components/entities/entity-board-view.tsx`; gallery expressed in pure template DSL `src/components/entities/entity-view-templates.ts:60`. All three are wired through the JSON→UI interpreter.
26	- **Form** — `DynamicSchemaForm` (`src/components/dynamic-schema-form.tsx:146`) renders text / number / boolean / enum-select / string-array inputs from the schema (incl. `required`, `readOnly`, `description` as label). Used for create (`src/components/create-entity-form.tsx:156`) and edit (`src/components/entity-tabs/index.tsx:167`).
27	- **Detail page** — `EntityTabsContent` (`src/components/entity-tabs/index.tsx:324`): read-only Overview (a `JsonRenderer` dashboard), relationships list, and the edit sidebar. `src/app/$owner/$.tsx:102` resolves the entity generically.
28	- **JSON→UI interpreter + plugin registry** — `JsonRenderer` (`src/lib/json-renderer/renderer.tsx`) interprets `{type, children, props}` trees with data bindings, `if`/`each` control flow, charts, tables, and app-registered nodes (`entity-table`, `entity-board`, `entity-link`, `entity-avatar`, `metric-series`) at `src/components/entities/renderer-registry.tsx:144`. Types may ship **authored type-level templates** (`view_templates` on the type, `src/lib/api/entities.ts:267`) and per-entity dashboard tabs (`entity.json_template`, rendered at `src/components/entity-tabs/index.tsx:385-428`), composed by server-run data sources.
29	
30	The enforcement evidence is the `manage_entity`/`manage_entity_schema` server tools the hooks call (`src/lib/api/entities.ts:603,676,700`), which are data-driven, not per-type endpoints. A **GUESS-free** check: creating a new entity type via `EntityTypeForm` (`src/components/settings/entity-types/entity-type-form.tsx:76`) makes a new list screen, detail screen, edit form, and sidebar entry appear with zero frontend code (sidebar: `src/components/sidebar/app-sidebar.tsx:346-433` lists `useEntityTypes` dynamically).
31	
32	## 3. Form / list-view / filter builders, column chooser, saved views, admin CRUD
33	
34	- **Form builder: YES (flat)** — `SchemaBuilder` (`src/components/settings/entity-types/schema-builder/schema-builder.tsx:173`), visual + raw-JSON modes. Visual mode is explicitly restricted to a flat object of primitives + enums (`isSimpleSchema`, `schema-builder.tsx:40-55`); nested objects/arrays/`oneOf` force JSON mode (`schema-builder.tsx:318-325`). No conditional/grouped layout, no line-item child schema.
35	- **List-view builder: PARTIAL** — the table/board/gallery switcher is a fixed built-in set plus authored `view_templates` (server-stored), but there is **no visual builder** for those templates (they're JSON authored server-side), and the switcher override is **session-only, never persisted** (`entity-type-list-panel.tsx:102` "session-only — never persisted").
36	- **Column chooser: NO** — columns = whatever the schema marks `x-table-column`; no per-user show/hide/reorder/width. Only the board has a group-by column toggle (`src/components/entities/entity-board-view.tsx:377`).
37	- **Filter builder: NO for entity lists** — a single free-text search box (`entity-type-list-panel.tsx:413-418`) + server-side sort; no field filter builder, no saved filters. The rich `clf_*`/`ClassificationFilters` machinery (`src/lib/filter-utils.ts`, `src/lib/event-filters.ts`) applies **only** to the Events stream, not entity lists.
38	- **Saved views: NO** — nothing persists a list configuration.
39	- **Admin CRUD scaffold: YES for types** — create/edit/delete/audit-history of entity types (`src/components/settings/entity-types/entity-type-page.tsx:25`, `:98` history) and relationship-type rules (`src/components/settings/entity-types/relationship-types-tab.tsx`). This is the nearest thing to a "resource admin".
40	
41	## 4. Adding a new screen — two paths and touch points
42	
43	**Schema-driven path (the one that matters for 441 screens):** define a new entity type at `/$owner/memory?create_type=true` → `EntityTypeForm` → server `manage_entity_schema`. The list (`/owner/<type>`), detail (`/owner/<type>/<slug>`), edit form, sidebar entry, schema-graph node all render automatically. **Touch points in `packages/owletto`: 0 code files.** (Verified end-to-end in code: route at `$entityType/index.tsx`, panel at `entity-type-list-panel.tsx`, form at `dynamic-schema-form.tsx`, detail at `entity-tabs/index.tsx`.)
44	
45	**Hand-built path (for Lobu's own sections):** a concrete example is the agent guardrails screen (`src/app/$owner/agents/$agentId/guardrails/*.tsx`). Files that must change:
46	1. Route file(s) under `src/app/$owner/…` using `createFileRoute` (auto-registered into `src/routeTree.gen.ts` by the TanStack router plugin — `tsr.config.json`).
47	2. Page component(s) — e.g. `src/components/agents/agent-guardrails-index.tsx`.
48	3. API hooks in `src/lib/api/*.ts` via `createOrgQuery`/`createMutation` (`src/lib/api/hook-factory.ts`) naming a server tool.
49	4. Nav wiring — `OWNER_SECTIONS` in `src/lib/owner-sections.ts` + the sidebar in `src/components/sidebar/app-sidebar.tsx`.
50	5. A smoke-test case in `src/app/__smoke__/all-routes.test.tsx` (route param fixtures + expected text, `all-routes.test.tsx:30`).
51	6. (Server, out of scope) a corresponding tool registration in `packages/server`.
52	
53	So a bespoke screen is ~5–6 touch points of hand-written React; a schema-driven screen is zero.
54	
55	## 5. Data-entry ergonomics
56	
57	- **Keyboard-driven grid entry: NO.** `EntityTableView` is read-only (sort + paginate + link out); editing is a separate sidebar form. No cell editing, no Enter-to-move-between-cells, no explicit tab order (browser default DOM order only; the one `tabIndex` in the entities dir is the graph view, `entity-type-graph-view.tsx:625`).
58	- **Inline add/edit rows: PARTIAL.** Single-record edit via the sidebar `DynamicSchemaForm` (save disabled until dirty, `entity-tabs/index.tsx:86,256`). Board drag = inline "move", `entity-board-view.tsx`. Click-to-edit primitives exist (`src/lib/editable-field/editable-primitive.tsx:40`) but are wired for agent-correction flows (`onCorrection` in `JsonRenderer`), not the entity grid. No inline "add row to a grid".
59	- **Master-detail (header + lines): NO.** Entities are flat records with JSONB `metadata`; `parent_id`/children give a hierarchy (parent column in list, `entity-table-view.tsx:403`), and typed relationships are **displayed read-only** (`src/components/memory/entity-relationships-panel.tsx:12-17` — "what IS linked, not what MAY be"). There is no editable line-item grid (no document header + lines pattern anywhere in the generic surface).
60	- **Lookup/autocomplete pickers: PARTIAL.** The generic form offers only an enum `<Select>` (`dynamic-schema-form.tsx:211-245`). A generic `Combobox` exists (`src/components/ui/combobox.tsx`) but only bespoke screens use it (member-picker, connector-selector, model-selector). Tables can *display* cross-linked entities (`x-link-entity-type`, `entity-table-view.tsx:201`) but the form cannot *pick* a related entity — no entity lookup control.
61	- **Validation display: PARTIAL.** Required-marker `*` + disabled Save (`dynamic-schema-form.tsx:217`, `entity-tabs/index.tsx:256`); server errors surface in a red box (`create-entity-form.tsx:166`). No per-field error annotations, no format/length/range checks client-side.
62	- **Unsaved-change guards: NO.** Dirty state only disables the Save button; there is **no** `beforeunload`, route blocker, or confirm-on-leave anywhere (grep for `beforeunload|useBlocker` = zero matches).
63	
64	## 6. Printing and document output
65	
66	**NO.** No PDF generation, no print layouts, no report templates, no Excel/CSV import or export anywhere in `packages/owletto`. The only `.pdf` string is a test fixture attachment (`src/mcp-apps/review/main.tsx:103`). The chart/data-table widgets render on-screen only; there is no download/serialize path. (Charts exist: `src/lib/json-renderer/charts/*`, ECharts-based.)
67	
68	## 7. Localization / i18n
69	
70	**NO.** No translation layer, no i18n library in `package.json`; all UI strings are hard-coded English literals in components. Locale is hard-coded `en-US` for dates in the two generic renderers (`src/components/entities/entity-table-view.tsx:593`, `src/lib/json-renderer/format-value.ts:58`). A Turkish UI would be a from-scratch extraction pass (feasible; purely mechanical, ~200 component files).
71	
72	## 8. Offline / latency / optimistic updates
73	
74	**NO offline mode, NO optimistic mutations.** Data is react-query with modest stale times (30s list, 60s type — `src/lib/api/entities.ts:671,760`), SSE-driven invalidation (`src/lib/use-invalidation-sse.ts`), and server-side sort/pagination/search (list params in `useEntitiesByType`, `entities.ts:603`). All writes await `mutateAsync` and flip `isPending` (no `onMutate`/`setQueryData` anywhere in `src/lib/api`). The single exception is the board's drag: optimistic move with per-entity rollback on error (`entity-board-view.tsx:409-412`). Nothing survives offline; an ERP's latency-sensitive data entry is fully server-round-trip.
75	
76	---
77	
78	## VERDICT
79	
80	| Capability | Rating | Effort to close gap |
81	|---|---|---|
82	| Schema-driven list/grid renderer (arbitrary type) | **YES** | exists; extend for ERP → MECHANICAL |
83	| Schema-driven form renderer | **PARTIAL** (flat scalars; no lines/lookups/date/image) | **HARD** |
84	| Form/list-view/filter builders, column chooser, saved views | **PARTIAL** (flat form-builder only; no list/filter/chooser/views) | **HARD** |
85	| Adding a screen without hand-written React | **YES** (0 files per schema-defined type) | TRIVIAL (mechanism exists) |
86	| Data-entry ergonomics (keyboard grid, inline rows, master-detail, lookups, unsaved guards) | **NO** (single-record edit + read-only relations only) | **HARD** |
87	| Printing / PDF / Excel | **NO** (no infra at all) | **HARD** |
88	| i18n / Turkish UI | **NO** (hard-coded English, `en-US` dates) | MECHANICAL |
89	| Offline / optimistic updates | **NO** (server-round-trip writes; board-only optimistic) | MECHANICAL |
90	
91	**Bottom line.** The decisive precondition — "screen renders from a schema, not from hand-built code" — is met in kind and in production shape: 441 Prodma screens would not be 441 React files, they'd be ~441 entity-type/schema/template definitions plus data. But the generic form and grid are **flat-scalar only**: no master-detail line grids, no entity-lookup fields, no per-field filters, no column chooser/saved views, no keyboard grid entry, no unsaved-change guards, no PDF/Excel, no Turkish. Those are buildable additions on top of the existing `JsonRenderer`/`DynamicSchemaForm`/`EntityTableView` foundation and **conflict with no documented AGENTS.md invariant** (nothing is ARCHITECTURAL). The honest answer: *structurally feasible as a schema-driven app builder, and a long way short of transactional ERP depth today.* The hard core of the gap is one thing — there is no generic "document with editable line items" abstraction — and nearly every other NO (filters, chooser, saved views, lookups, grid editing) hangs off that missing master-detail primitive. **(GUESS:** I did not run the app; all findings are from reading the shipped code paths above, which are consistent and well-tested.)**

Lobu side is complete and I've verified its load-bearing claims against source. Prodma side: 6 of 8 in, `arch` and `stok` still running.

## Where Lobu lacks — the verified answer

**What's genuinely there** (this surprised me upward):

Schema-driven UI is real and in production shape. Define an entity type and you get a list view, detail page, edit form, and sidebar entry with **zero frontend files changed** — board and gallery views too, columns derived from `x-table-column` schema annotations. So the 441-screen problem is not 441 React files. That was the make-or-break question and it passed.

Underneath, the plumbing is solid: transactions with real locking (63 `pg_advisory` call sites), soft delete, idempotency, partial unique indexes, at-least-once scheduling, encrypted secrets with a hard worker/credential boundary, and **on-premise deployment via compose and Helm** — which matters more than it sounds for a manufacturer who won't put financials in someone else's cloud. External HTTP integration with credentials is a YES, so an e-Fatura provider is reachable.

**What blocks an ERP**, ranked:

1. **`entities.metadata` is a JSONB blob.** Every business field lives in one untyped column. Validation is app-level AJV against the JSON-Schema; the database enforces nothing. Prodma has 503 tables and **1,175 foreign keys** — port that and all 1,175 become app-level conventions with no database backstop. This is the deepest issue and it's not a UI problem.
2. **No master-detail primitive.** There is no "document header + editable line items" abstraction anywhere. An invoice *is* a header plus lines. The UI agent's sharpest observation is that nearly every other UI gap — no inline row editing, no keyboard grid entry, no entity-lookup fields — hangs off this one missing thing.
3. **No field-level authorization.** Prodma ships `YETKI_ALANLAR` today. Lobu's only masking is secret/Sentry redaction; I checked every `redact|mask` hit and none touch business data. Rated HARD. **Row-level scoping is rated ARCHITECTURAL** — the only ARCHITECTURAL rating in the whole audit. Also: the write-gate is agent-centric by design, and humans are explicitly never gated.
4. **No documents.** No PDF, no print layouts, no Excel/CSV import or export anywhere. Invoices and dispatch notes must print — this is non-optional, and it's also how e-Fatura output gets produced.
5. **No i18n.** Hard-coded English strings, `en-US` dates. Turkish UI is a from-scratch extraction across ~200 components. Mechanical, but real.
6. **No bulk import path.** The Postgres connector is read-only at 5k rows/sync. Migrating an existing ERP dataset has no route today.
7. **No gapless document numbering** — but this one's easy. Advisory locks are already used in 63 places; it's a counter row and a lock.

The two agents that never spoke to each other — `data` and `ops` — independently landed on the same sentence: **Lobu around an ERP, not as the ERP.** When separately-scoped audits converge like that, it's usually right.

## What this means for your goal

You wanted to prove Lobu covers everything Prodma covers. The honest finding is that it doesn't today, and the gap isn't configuration — it's a product layer to be built: an ERP data plane, a document/lines abstraction, a human permission axis, and a printing stack. Notably, **none of it violates a documented Lobu invariant** except row-level scoping. So "can Lobu get there" is a roadmap question, not an architecture-blocker question.

That's actually a better outcome for you than a clean yes. A gap list this specific is the roadmap deliverable you asked for, and it's defensible in front of someone who runs the real system.

**Confidence: 85 on the Lobu gaps** — basis: I independently verified the decisive claims against source (entities DDL from `db/migrations/00000000000000_baseline.sql`, absence of PDF/Excel/i18n/unsaved-guard libraries, the redaction hits, 63 advisory-lock sites, write-gate call sites). Not verified: nobody ran the app, so all findings are static reads. **Confidence: 40 on the Prodma side** — 6 reports landed but I haven't read them yet.

**Next actions:**
1. I read the 6 Prodma reports and synthesize both sides into the gap report — the main deliverable.
2. Decide whether the master-detail/line-items primitive is worth prototyping in Lobu, since it unblocks the largest cluster of gaps at once.
3. Ask the owner what Prodma's actual e-Fatura integration is (which integrator) — the `muhasebe` agent may have found it, but the source dump may not contain it.
4. Clean up when you're done: `_analysis/` in the project dir and the `prodma-gap-audit` worktree.

content.text:
You're right on most of these. Point by point.

**1. JSONB — I over-called it. Withdrawing.** `validateEntityMetadata` runs AJV Draft-7 on create (`manage_entity.ts:274`) *and* update (`:434`), so types, `required`, formats and enums are enforced at write. Uniqueness on a metadata field is a functional unique index, and there's already precedent in the baseline: `idx_entities_metadata_domain ON entities ((metadata->>'domain'), organization_id)`. Invoice-number uniqueness is one index. And referential integrity is real — `entity_relationships` carries actual FKs to `entities(id)` with `ON DELETE CASCADE` on both ends. What's genuinely left is much smaller: changing a schema doesn't retro-validate existing rows, there are no CHECK constraints for cross-field invariants ("discount ≤ line total"), and an 8-FK invoice becomes 8 relationship rows rather than 8 columns — write amplification and heavier joins. At 20 users, none of that is fatal.

**2. parent/child — the model's fine; the gap is atomicity.** `parent_id` is real (185 references) and relationships are typed, so header/lines is representable. But `manage_entity.ts` has **zero transaction usage** — no `begin`, no `sql.begin`. An invoice header plus 20 lines is 21 independent writes, and a crash on line 12 leaves half an invoice. That's the actual problem, and it's far narrower than "no master-detail primitive": the transaction API and advisory locks already exist elsewhere in the codebase, just not on this path. The UI half — an inline line-item grid — is still genuinely missing.

**3. Relationships for authz — modeling yes, enforcement no.** You could model "rep → allowed customers" as relationship rows. Nothing reads them on the human path. `manage_entity.ts:125` says it outright: *"Entity read gate for agents/watchers. Humans skip (role ACL is separate)."* The gate exists and deliberately doesn't apply to people. Field-level masking is a different thing again — stripping keys from `metadata` on read by role — and nothing does that anywhere. So this one stands, restated: an enforcement gap on the human read path, not a modeling gap. It's also the only item the audit rated ARCHITECTURAL.

**4. `x-file` — you're right, that's in-pattern.** The vocabulary is real and extensible: `x-currency`, `x-image`, `x-measure`, `x-dimension`, `x-link-entity-type`, `x-link-lookup-field`, `x-table-relationships`. `x-image` already exists. Worth noting `x-link-entity-type` means entity lookups are already in the schema vocabulary. But my gap wasn't attachments — it was *generating* the invoice. An e-Fatura is a deterministic templated XML/PDF with legally fixed layout; that's a rendering stack, and specifically not something an LLM should compose. Restating this one as **document generation**, not files.

**5. i18n — conceded.** If chat is the primary interface, English storage with translation on demand is a legitimate design and I shouldn't have listed UI i18n as a blocker. The residual isn't UI: an invoice handed to a customer or filed with GİB must be Turkish and exact. That folds into #4. Dropping it as a separate gap.

**7. Gapless numbering — what it is.** Turkish invoices carry a series plus a sequential number (*fatura seri/sıra no*), and the tax authority expects the sequence unbroken — every number issued must be accounted for. Two ways it breaks: you allocate a number and the save then fails, burning it and leaving a hole; or two users save at once, `MAX(n)+1` hands both the same number, and you've issued a duplicate. The fix is a counter row plus a lock so allocation and commit succeed or fail together. This is the easy one — 63 `pg_advisory` sites already exist, so it's a day's work. It only earns a mention because "we'll fix it later" is exactly how you end up unable to explain invoice 4,412 to an auditor.

**Revised gap list** — five items, and only one is architectural:

| # | Gap | Severity |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | No atomic multi-row write on the entity path | Real, fixable — primitives exist |

content.text:
Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page — what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first — CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world — its materials, instruments, vernacular — is where distinctive choices come from. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. The Artifact CSP blocks font CDNs, so don't link a webfont URL and risk a silent fallback. Instead inline the face as a @font-face data URI. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject — the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states, not two: an explicit choice stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting stamps *nothing* — most viewers see the un-stamped document, where only `prefers-color-scheme` separates light from dark. Structure the CSS token-level for all three: the bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice beats a dark OS; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also wins in the other direction. Style components through the tokens, never directly inside a media or `[data-theme]` block — a color whose only definition sits behind `[data-theme]` never applies in the un-stamped state, and the page renders one theme's text on the other theme's ground. Two more rules keep each theme resolving as a set: the artifact composites over a ground the viewer paints in *its* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token — a transparent body silently borrows the host's ground; and every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never a literal that only works in one theme. Before publishing, scan the stylesheet for any color declared only inside a media or `[data-theme]` block — that is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first — don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme — then skip the media query and stamps entirely but still paint the background and every color explicitly, so the page holds on either host ground; make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content — tables, code, diagrams — gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks; visual bugs hide in the gap between source and output. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out — a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen — name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it — no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Name the page like a product, not a caption.** The `<title>` is the artifact's name in the gallery and the browser tab, and it sets the reader's first impression of care. Give the page a real name: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific to the subject — or, for a page that exists to answer one question, that question itself, which is then the page's name. Stop at the name — a title that carries its own explainer after a dash or colon reads as generated filler. The name must also identify the page among many: in the gallery it sits beside dozens of other artifacts, and a generic category label that could sit on any of them fails as a name just as surely as an appended explainer. When a candidate title pairs the name with a generic word — a greeting, a category, a page-type label — the name is the half to keep; a trim that drops the identity and keeps the generic word produces exactly the title that could sit on any page. And the rule removes explainers, it does not impose brevity: a multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished, and shortening it further only makes it generic. The one-sentence publish `description` is where the explanation belongs; the gallery shows it right under the title.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number — a pill, a chip, a severity stripe — so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan — a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles — a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world — headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

Design plan before I build:

**Palette** — cool paper `#FAFAFB`, ink `#151A22`, muted `#606B7B`, hairline `#DDE1E7`, accent deep teal `#0F6E66`; severity ramp separate from accent (blocked `#9E2B25`, hard `#B06520`, mechanical `#37658F`, trivial `#4B7B4F`). **Type** — system sans for prose, monospace as the identity face for eyebrows, labels and all figures; no webfonts (CSP would silently fall back). **Layout** — spec-sheet: hairline rules, 68ch prose, full-bleed data tables, squared severity chips rather than pills.

Feasibility assessment · 13 August 2026

Prodma on Lobu

Can Lobu replace a 20-year-old Turkish manufacturing ERP? A capability-by-capability comparison against the real system — 503 tables, 441 screens, and the parts nobody can port.

Subject Prodma — .NET WinForms + SQL Server Industry Automotive injection moulding Scale <20 concurrent users Method 12 parallel code-audit agents, claims spot-verified

Bottom line

Feasible in kind. Not in completeness — yet.

The decisive question was whether 441 screens means 441 hand-built screens. It does not. Prodma already drives 207 of them from a table-driven CRUD engine, and Lobu renders any entity type from a JSON-Schema with zero frontend files changed. Both systems are schema-driven admins. That is the strongest single finding here.

What Lobu lacks is not architecture — it is a product layer: document printing, Excel, atomic multi-row writes, and per-user grid state. Of seven identified gaps, six are ordinary engineering and one is genuinely hard. None conflict with a documented Lobu invariant.

The exception is statutory. Turkish e-Fatura, KDV declarations and BA/BS reporting cannot be ported by any platform — they are government integrations that must be rebuilt or re-licensed regardless of what you build on.

Section 01 · What Prodma actually is

Measured, not estimated

Every figure below was counted directly from the source dump and from a live M_MENU export, not inferred.

503live database tables
441distinct end-user screens
1.63Mlines of C#
25%of that is dead duplicates
153columns on CARI alone
11top-level modules

Two facts about the codebase shape everything else. The team versioned by filename, not git — there are 134 date-suffixed files and 23 Copy of… files, including roughly fifteen dated copies of ListeYap.cs at 11,000–25,000 lines each. And the live schema is one generated file, so the data model is recoverable without reading the 1.6M lines.

Parts of the live system are missing from the dump. The invoice-number generator GetMax_Fatura_No lives in a DLL that was not included. So do the credit-limit predicates, the cheque-portfolio validator, the period-close voucher generation, the RDLC report assets, and the GİB e-invoice proxies. These must be recovered from the original solution or re-derived from database behaviour — a cost any replacement pays, on any platform.

Section 02 · The decomposition

441 screens are not 441 problems

Classifying every screen by what it actually does is the number that decides feasibility. Prodma's own engineers reached the same conclusion two decades ago and built a generic CRUD engine for the bulk of it.

Screen classCountWhat it isPort cost
Config-driven CRUD207 TanitimSablon forms generated from an ALANLAR field table — master data, lookups, definitions Mechanical
Hand-coded reports142 ListeYap.XxxList methods — balance matching, forecasting, price comparison, inside 25k-line files Hard
Real business logic~113 Documents, postings, MRP, pricing, costing — the screens where rules live Hard

Lobu's equivalent of the 207 is already built and arguably better: define an entity type and the list view, detail page, edit form, board view and sidebar entry all appear with no frontend code written at all. Columns, formatting, currency and cross-entity links are driven by x-* schema annotations.

Section 03 · Module verdicts

Where the difficulty actually sits

Eight parallel audits, one per module. Difficulty is dominated by pricing, document chains and costing — not by volume of screens.

ModuleScreensHardest capabilityVerdict
Cari (customers, AR)84Customer pricing — 10 FIYAT_* tables, two engines that already disagree with each otherHard
Stok / Ambar63Stock costing and valuation on backdated documentsHard
Alış / Satış34Document chain and numbering — three incompatible Max+1 schemesHard
Muhasebe23e-Fatura via GİB; VUK depreciation rules that change yearlyBlocked
Üretim / MRP23Two-stage production costing with cost-centre redistributionHard
Sistem36Multi-company as physically separate databases per fiscal yearHard
Sipariş / Teklif16Order lifecycle — small state machine, easyMechanical
Araçlar / platform35Pre-printed stationery position printing; RF handheld workflowHard

Section 04 · The gap list

What Lobu would have to build

Ranked by what would actually block adoption, not by engineering interest. Every one of these was verified against Lobu's source, not assumed.

01

Document generation and printing

No PDF, no print layouts, no templating anywhere in Lobu. Prodma prints onto pre-printed multi-copy stationery with a user-maintainable field-position table. Invoices and dispatch notes must print, and this is also how e-Fatura output is produced.

Hard
02

Excel import and export

A 53-file footprint in Prodma and the owner's daily working habit. Lobu has no Excel or CSV path in either direction. Mechanically easy, but a platform that weakens this gets rejected regardless of every other strength.

Mechanical
03

Atomic multi-row writes

The entity write path runs no transaction, so an invoice header plus 20 lines is 21 independent writes — a crash midway leaves half a document. The transaction API and advisory locks already exist elsewhere in the codebase; they are simply not on this path.

Mechanical
04

Per-user grid state

Prodma gives every user saved column layouts, saved filters and per-user list templates. Lobu has no column chooser, no filter builder and no saved views; a view switch is session-only and never persisted. This is what daily ERP users notice first.

Mechanical
05

Row-scope enforcement for humans

Lobu's entity read gate applies to agents and behaviours; humans skip it by design. Expressing "a rep sees only their own customers" is possible via typed relationships, but nothing enforces it on the human read path today.

Hard
06

Bulk data import

The Postgres connector is read-only at 5,000 rows per sync. There is no route for loading an existing ERP dataset. Accepted as a known limitation.

Mechanical
07

Gapless document numbering

Turkish invoices carry an unbroken series and sequence; a burned or duplicated number is an audit question. Lobu has no allocator, but 63 advisory-lock call sites already exist — this is a counter row and a lock.

Trivial

Section 05 · Statutory

The part no platform can port

These are government integrations, not features. They must be rebuilt against GİB or licensed from an integrator whatever the underlying system — so they are a cost of the project, not a mark against Lobu.

ObligationState in ProdmaStatus
e-Fatura / e-Arşiv / e-İrsaliyeDE-GA SOAP integrator; generated proxies absent from the dumpBlocked
KDV declaration (beyanname)Rates and tevkifat posting exist; declaration prep does notBlocked
BA / BS formsTable and stub only; threshold logic never writtenBlocked
VUK depreciation + enflasyon düzeltmesiComplete engine, but encodes rules that change annuallyHard
Tekdüzen Hesap PlanıConfig data, not logic — a hierarchical account tableMechanical

Section 06 · Findings that cut the other way

Prodma is weaker than its reputation in four places

A fair assessment has to record where the incumbent is not actually delivering what its table names suggest. Each of these lowers the bar a replacement must clear.

  • Field-level permissions are cosmetic. YETKI_ALANLAR is applied as .Visible = false on WinForms controls across 1,245 call sites. Anyone reaching the database sees every column. This is UI hiding, not a security control.
  • Authentication is plaintext passwords. No AD, no LDAP, nothing to preserve.
  • The MRP run is a stub that returns null. Lead-time offsetting has fields and data but no computation. Capacity is ignored entirely.
  • The scheduler is broken by default — dead due-checker, no watchdog, no duplicate prevention. Several "port this" items are really "build this properly for the first time."

Add to these the two pricing engines that already disagree with each other, a dangling production-costing reference, and hardcoded customer IDs inside a sector-specific fork. A replacement does not need to match Prodma at 100% — it needs to match what is actually used and actually correct.

Section 07 · Method and confidence

What was verified versus assumed

Twelve code-audit agents ran in parallel — eight over the Prodma source, four over Lobu — each scoped to one module or capability and required to cite files and rate port difficulty. Their claims were not taken at face value: the load-bearing ones were re-checked directly against source.

  • Verified independently: the entities table DDL and its JSONB shape; schema validation on both create and update; foreign keys with cascade on typed relationships; absence of PDF, Excel, i18n and unsaved-change libraries; 63 advisory-lock sites; the human-skips-the-read-gate comment; the 1,245 UI-hiding call sites.
  • Measured, not estimated: all file, line, table and screen counts, derived from the source tree and the live M_MENU export joined against the entity model.
  • Not verified: nobody ran either application. Every finding is a static read. Two Prodma module audits — inventory and cross-cutting architecture — had not returned when this was written.

Two claims made early in this analysis were wrong and are corrected here. Field-level authorization was initially rated an architectural blocker; it is client-side UI hiding. And the menu was described as per-user and per-region customizable based on table names; the code shows those tables are dead.

Section 08 · Open questions

What would sharpen this next

  • Row counts per table from the live database. One query would separate the used tables from the abandoned ones and materially tighten the 113-screen estimate.
  • The YETKI tables, exported like M_MENU was. The permission model is currently read from code, not from what the customer actually configured.
  • Which e-Fatura integrator contract is live. DE-GA appears in the source, but the proxies are missing — the commercial arrangement determines whether this is an integration or a procurement.
  • Whether the master-detail primitive gets built. Header-plus-editable-lines is the one abstraction that unblocks the largest cluster of remaining gaps at once.

Assessment prepared 13 August 2026 from a source dump dated to June 2026 and a live M_MENU export. Figures are counts, not projections. Difficulty ratings are engineering judgement and should be re-tested against a working slice before anyone commits a schedule to them.

**Your pushback changed the report substantially.** Four of my seven original gaps were wrong or overstated, and the corrections are written into the document rather than quietly dropped — Section 07 names both mistakes explicitly. **What the agents found that neither of us predicted:** Excel is the owner's daily workflow across 53 files, and Lobu has no path in either direction — the `platform` agent's judgement was that weakening it gets the platform rejected regardless of every other strength. Report updated at the same URL: **https://claude.ai/code/artifact/b65a24ee-a91d-4a7e-a364-e881ed9c7cd0**

## What the YETKI export gave us

Seven sheets: the menu again, two enum lookups, and the three permission tables I'd asked for.

**The field-permission gap is far smaller than I assessed.** Prodma's entire field-authorization vocabulary is four states — `GOSTERILECEK` (shown), `GOSTERILMEYECEK` (hidden), `SADECE GOSTERILECEK` (display-only), `EK ALAN` (extra field). Lobu's schema form **already honours `readOnly`** (`dynamic-schema-form.tsx:203`), so display-only maps directly. Reaching parity means adding a hidden state, not building a security layer.

**The field-type gap is exactly three.** Prodma's CRUD engine supports nine types; Lobu already renders six of them. Missing: `TARIH` (date), `TARIHSAAT` (datetime), `BAGLI_ALAN` (linked field — the entity lookup I flagged earlier). That's a much sharper statement than "flat scalars only," and it's a week of work rather than an architecture problem.

**The best find is the operation catalog.** `YETKI_ISLEM_TANITIM` is a named, coded inventory of business verbs — `Teklif_Siparis_Olustur` (create order from quote), `Siparis_Irsaliye_Olustur` (raise dispatch note), `Toplu_Faturalama` (bulk invoicing), `Entegrasyon_Boz` (reverse an accounting posting), `Siparis_Kapama_Satir` (close an order line). At least 170 distinct codes.

That's worth more to you than the permission data it came from. It's a pre-written list of what the business actually *does*, in the exact shape Lobu models as operations — and therefore the exact list of what an agent could be given the ability to invoke. If you build the pitch around "here are your 170 operations, now an agent can run them," that list came from their own database, not from us.

**One caveat that matters:** sheets 4, 5 and 6 each stop at exactly 201 rows. Those are `TOP 200` exports, so 170 operations is a floor, not a total. Worth asking for them untruncated — a `SELECT COUNT(*)` on each would tell us how far off we are.

`arch` is still running; everything else has landed.

**Confidence: 90 on the permission-model decode** — basis: the enum sheets are unambiguous and I verified the `readOnly` support and the rendered field types directly in Lobu's form component. The column *meanings* in sheets 4 and 6 are inferred from value patterns (the dominant `True,False,False,False` reading as view-only), not from column headers — the export has none. **Unchanged elsewhere.**

**Next actions:**
1. Ask for sheets 4/5/6 untruncated, plus column headers — the header row would confirm my flag interpretation rather than leaving it inferred.
2. Take the 170 operation codes as the spine of the working slice: pick the order-to-cash subset and implement those as real Lobu operations.
3. Add date, datetime and entity-lookup to `DynamicSchemaForm` — smallest concrete unlock on the list, and it makes the 207 CRUD screens genuinely portable.
4. Table row counts still outstanding, and still the single highest-value query.

## PORT VERDICT

- **Data-access patterns (EF per-call contexts + raw SQL side-channels):** MECHANICAL — the three generations are readable and map cleanly onto one repository layer; the ~270 inline writes and 32 `SqlCommand` files are enumerable, but every call site must be re-expressed against a typed model.
- **Service/Cntrl/Vm CRUD tier:** TRIVIAL to MECHANICAL — 706 VMs + 419 Services + 362 Cntrls follow one template (`AService`/`BaseCtrl`); they are the single most automatable part of the port (grid metadata in `M_ALANLAR` even supplies field lists).
- **Report/query engine (ListeYapBase/ListService, ~46k lines + CariGrupBilgileriAl*):** HARD — hundreds of report methods encode business definitions of balances/aging/margin directly in LINQ with no spec; each must be re-derived against a live DB to verify numbers match.
- **Voucher posting logic (StokFisHelper/MuhasebeFisHelper/FisOrtakService + Fis forms):** HARD — correctness-critical, fused to DevExpress grid events, and written as sequential non-atomic commits with sector- and client-specific branches (`Gemi`/`DEGA`); it must be re-derived, not extracted.
- **Transaction/concurrency behavior:** HARD — Prodma has *none* (no transactions, no locking, no concurrency detection, single-client globals); re-implementing it correctly (true atomic posting, stale-write detection, per-user state) is additive work a port must design from scratch, not translate.
- **e-invoice / e-archive / e-irsaliye transmission (GIB integrations):** STATUTORY-BLOCKED — direct GIB/Payflex web-service client code (eFaturaYazService.cs, eArsivYazService.cs, eIrsaliyeGonderService.cs) must be re-certified against current Turkish Revenue Administration schemas and envelopes; this is legal integration, not application logic.
- **Schema evolution / user-defined fields (`M_ALANLAR`, `ALTER TABLE` at runtime):** HARD — the database is partly self-describing and user-extensible at runtime (TabloEkle.cs, DbAlanIslemleri.cs); any replacement must reproduce a metadata-driven dynamic-entity capability or the existing 153-column entity monoliths won't map.
########## composition estimate ##########
## 6. CODE COMPOSITION ESTIMATE

Basis: 1,634,654 total LOC across 5,598 `.cs`; DevExpress decompiled 30,113 (678 files); `*.Designer.cs` generated UI 503,940 (~31% of all LOC, ~44% of the non-DevExpress product); live product code (excl. Designer + dated dups + eski/Copy) ≈ **637k LOC in 4,183 files**; dead duplicates ≈ **460-470k (~28%)**, matching the brief's "25% dead". Estimates below are of the live product (~637k):

- **(a) Generated UI / Designer:** ~31% of product (mostly `*.Designer.cs`; plus `ProdmaModel.Views.cs` 26k and the EF entity classes, e.g. `CARI.cs` 153 columns + 169 nav props, are generated-shaped).
- **(b) Reporting / printing:** ~25%. Report engine alone (`ListeYapBase` + `ListService` + `ListeIslemleri` + `QueryOlustur` + `*Listeleri*` + `ListHelper`) ≈ 110k (~17%); on top, 95 files use `PrintDocument`/`XtraReport` and 297 call `Print/ShowPrintPreview`, incl. custom GDI printing engines like `FaturaYazService` (DrawString-by-coordinate invoice print) and label printers in `OrtakIslemlerService` (EtiketYazdir...).
- **(c) CRUD plumbing:** ~35%. Services 135k + Cntrls 35k + Vms 32k + Enums 373 + entity classes + the generic `AService`/`BaseCtrl`/`FisSablonSon`/`TanitimSablon` scaffolding. Most Service/Cntrl LOC is mechanical mapping + projections, not rules.
- **(d) Genuinely non-trivial business rules:** ~8-12%, concentrated in a small set of files: `FiyatBulService` (price cascade + FX), `StokFisSatirCntrl` / `CariCntrl` (limits, KDV tolerance, sector/firm rules), `StokFisHelper`/`MuhasebeFisHelper`/`SiparisFisHelper`/`FaturaHelper`/`FisOrtakService`/`FisControlService` (posting/validation), `OrtakIslemlerService` (bulk transfers/import), `DevirDuzeltmeService` (balance correction), `YardimciIslemler` (financial math, number-to-text), the e-invoice trio (`eFaturaYazService`, `eArsivYazService`, `eIrsaliyeGonderService`) and `MuhasebeHesapPlani.cs`.

So the honest split: **most LOC is CRUD plumbing and report queries; the genuinely hard rules are a minority of lines but the entire risk surface**, and they are the parts welded to grids/forms and written against the live schema without tests or transactions.

## The architecture pass changed two ratings

**Prodma is 637k lines, not 1.63M.** Strip the generated designer files, the decompiled DevExpress assemblies and the dead duplicates and you get 4,183 files of live code. Of that: 31% generated UI, 25% reporting and printing, 35% CRUD plumbing, and **8–12% genuinely non-trivial business rules** — roughly 50–75k lines. That slice is the entire risk surface, and the agent named the files: price resolution, voucher posting and validation, balance correction, the chart of accounts, financial arithmetic, the e-invoice trio. Everything else is volume.

That reframes the project. "Rewrite a 1.6M-line ERP" is a five-year sentence. "Re-derive 60k lines of rules and regenerate the rest from schema" is a real plan.

**Two corrections to my own gap list:**

*Atomic multi-row writes are no longer a parity gap.* I rated it Mechanical and put it third. Prodma has **no transactions at all** — no locking, no concurrency detection, single-client globals, voucher posting as a sequence of independent commits. Lobu isn't behind here; it's ahead, and using the transaction API it already has would make it the stricter system. Downgraded to an improvement.

*And one capability cuts the other way that I'd missed entirely.* Prodma's database is partly self-describing: an `M_ALANLAR` field table plus runtime `ALTER TABLE` lets users add their own fields without a code change. Any replacement has to reproduce that or the 153-column monoliths don't map. Lobu's schema-per-type over a JSONB column does it natively and without the DDL — which is the strongest technical argument in the report, and it came from the thing I originally called the deepest problem.

One nuance worth correcting: the e-invoice **client code is present** (`eFaturaYazService`, `eArsivYazService`, `eIrsaliyeGonderService`). It's the generated SOAP proxies that are missing, and the schemas that need re-certifying. Still statutory-blocked, but less of a black box than I implied.

**Confidence: 85 overall, unchanged in shape.** The counts are measured and the Lobu claims are independently verified. The composition percentages are the `arch` agent's estimate from file-group line counts — directionally sound, and I'd hold them to ±5 points rather than treat 8–12% as precise. Still nothing runtime-verified on either system.

**Next actions:**
1. Table row counts from the live DB — still outstanding, still the highest-value single query.
2. The named hard-rule files are now a concrete reading list. `FiyatBulService` is the one I'd read first; two pricing engines that disagree is the deepest correctness risk in the system.
3. Build the working slice around the order-to-cash operation codes, with date/datetime/entity-lookup added to the schema form as the enabling work.
4. Say the word and I'll clean up `_analysis/` and the `prodma-gap-audit` worktree — the twelve raw agent reports live there and are much more detailed than the published summary.

content.text:
Good challenges. Taking them in turn.

**Printing — you're right that I conflated two things.** File *storage* isn't hard and `x-file` covers it. The "hard" rating came from something specific: Prodma prints onto **pre-printed multi-copy stationery** using GDI+ `DrawString`-by-coordinate, with a user-maintainable field-position table (`FATURA_IRSALIYE_AYAR`). That's not "render a PDF" — it's "put this value at 47mm × 112mm on paper that already has the letterhead and carbon copies on it." Generic report designers handle that badly.

But that may be legacy. Turkish e-Fatura has largely displaced pre-printed invoice stationery — if they're on e-Fatura, the printed artifact is a PDF rendered from the invoice envelope, and the coordinate machinery is dead weight they've been carrying. **That's a real question for the owner**, and the answer moves this gap from Hard to Mechanical.

**Excel — agents are right for half of it.** Splitting the two directions:

*Export* is the weak case for agents. Users export the grid they're looking at — current filters, current columns, 5,000 rows — and they do it many times a day. Round-tripping that through a model is slow, costly and non-deterministic, when "download this view" is a few hours of work and always correct.

*Import* is the strong case. Messy spreadsheets with inconsistent headers and merged cells are exactly what LLMs are good at, and Prodma's OleDb import wizards are miserable by comparison. But loading 3,000 price rows has to be exact — a model mis-parsing three rows in a price list is a silent financial error nobody catches until a customer is invoiced wrong.

So the split is: **agent does the mapping, deterministic code does the transfer.** That's the reliable division, and it shrinks the gap considerably — Lobu doesn't need an Excel stack, it needs a deterministic XLSX/CSV read-write primitive that agents can drive. I'll re-rate it as a small lift rather than a first-party product surface.

**What I'd still want from the owner** — and it isn't data:

The highest-value thing is **an hour watching someone actually use it**. Which 10–15 of the 441 screens do people open every day, and what does a normal working day look like in them? That tells us more about what a replacement must nail than any table dump, and it's the one thing no amount of code reading recovers. Beyond that, three specific questions:

- Are you on e-Fatura, and do you still print onto pre-printed forms? (Decides the printing gap.)
- Which e-invoice integrator is the live contract? (Decides whether that's engineering or procurement.)
- Which screens do people export to Excel from, and what do they do with it afterwards? (The "afterwards" usually reveals a missing feature.)

Six agents are running now — four on the hard-rule files, two on Lobu's extensibility including the `json_renderer` registry. I'll build the full gap register with the workaround / small lift / big lift classification when they land.

## The register, in short

**Workarounds — no build at all (5):** Turkish UI via chat-first translation; messy-spreadsheet import via agent mapping; ad-hoc reporting via agent over the sandboxed read-only SQL data sources that already exist; field-level masking by omitting fields per type (parity, since Prodma's is UI-only anyway); approval flows via the durable approval cards already shipped.

**Small lifts — days to weeks, no architectural change (8):** the three missing field types; a deterministic XLSX/CSV primitive; gapless numbering; a transaction on the entity write path; a hidden-field state; threading `context.components`; persisted list config; a bulk import loader.

**Big lifts — worth discussing before building (5, plus statutory):** runtime third-party component registration; the editable line-item grid; row-scope enforcement for humans; document generation; and transactional posting inside the sandbox.

That last one is the conflict I'd flag hardest, because it isn't on anyone's list yet. Sandboxed code is where org-specific business rules would naturally live — it's the one place custom logic runs without a deploy. But **the sandbox has no transactions and caps at 180 seconds**. An ERP's rules are posting rules, and posting must be atomic. So either rules move out of the sandbox, or the sandbox gains a transaction boundary. Worth deciding deliberately rather than discovering halfway through the slice.

The seam is designed and in place.

Three things sit between that and your goal, and they're very different sizes. The override is **never passed** at the detail-page or event-card call sites — an afternoon's work to thread. Registration is a **compile-time object literal**, so a new component means shipping React — mechanical, but a deploy every time. Genuine third-party registration needs bundle delivery, a shared React instance and an org-scoped registry — that's the real project.

The encouraging half: template authoring is already solved. Admin-authored, structurally validated, versioned with rollback, backed by read-only org-scoped SQL. You don't need to build that. Only the component half is frozen at build time.

The money primitives depend on .NET Framework tie-to-even rounding, per-line rather than per-document rounding, and discount precision keyed to the company record. The audit's warning is worth quoting directly: any clean-up silently changes money. These functions should be ported as literal translations with tests pinned to known outputs — not improved, not tidied, not modernised.

content.text:
Verified, and these are the kind that survive your test.

## Three that an infinitely capable agent still can't fix

**1. Entity data changes leave no trace.** `manage_entity.ts` writes no event, no audit row — zero hits for any logging call. There's an `entity_type_audit` table with `before_payload`/`after_payload`, but it audits the **schema**, not the data. And `events` is not written on entity edit.

So when someone changes a customer's credit limit or an item's price, the old value is gone. No actor, no timestamp beyond `updated_at`, no before/after. An agent cannot recover a value that was never stored — this is the cleanest architectural gap in the system, and it's invisible until the first time someone asks "who changed this, and when?"

It also kills point-in-time entirely. "What was this customer's balance on 31 March" isn't a hard query here, it's an unanswerable one.

**2. Nothing can be made immutable.** A posted invoice is an ordinary mutable row. There's no frozen/posted concept, no state machine, no legal-transition enforcement — status is a metadata string and `manage_entity` will happily set it to anything. Period close can't be enforced because there's nothing to enforce it with. An agent can be *told* not to edit posted documents; it cannot be *prevented*.

**3. On `json_template` — this is the real ceiling, and it's subtler than I said.** You're right that templates plus JSON Schema cover forms. But there are two registries, not one: `components` and **`actions`** (`RendererAction`, `actions?: Record<string, RendererAction>`). Both are caller-supplied React callbacks, and **neither is supplied anywhere** — I grepped the entity and detail-page call sites and found nothing passing either.

That means a template can *reference* an action by name but cannot *define* one. So when a user asks the agent for new UI, the agent can compose any layout from the existing vocabulary and wire it to affordances that already exist in compiled code — but it cannot create a new behaviour. Generated UI is bounded by the action vocabulary someone shipped.

That's not an argument against the agentic model. It's the thing to design deliberately: **the action vocabulary is your real extensibility surface**, more than the component one. Ship the right verbs and agent-generated UI goes a very long way; ship the wrong ones and every new screen needs a deploy regardless of how good the generation is.

Four agents are digging on the remaining architectural questions — where deterministic transactional logic can run, whether a human enforcement plane exists at all, and whether write-time materialization scales to hundreds of ERP aggregates. Those three plus the above are, I think, the whole real list.

I've dropped e-Fatura, Excel, i18n, PDF, printing, report builders and form builders from the gap register entirely. I'll rewrite the report around the architectural set once the agents land.
