input.old_string: Also: extracting a route-private predicate into a small exported helper (e.g. `connectorRemoveState`) is a legitimate way to make gating logic testable, and is better factoring on its own merits. Flag it as a production change when reporting.
input.new_string:
**Two failure modes that make a mutation run WORTHLESS — check both every time:**

1. **The mutation silently did not apply.** A `perl`/`replace` that matches
   nothing leaves the file unchanged, so the suite passes and looks like the
   test has no teeth — when in fact nothing was tested. Happened three times
   (M3, N2, and once targeting a `LIKE` form the code no longer used). **Assert
   the text changed**: `assert OLD in s` before writing, and `grep -c` after.
   A green mutation run must be DISCARDED, never counted, unless the edit is
   proven to have landed.
2. **The assertion passes by a margin too thin to trust.** A test that catches a
   mutation by a 1 ms timestamp delta would falsely pass whenever two
   transactions land in the same millisecond. Fix by making it an exact-value
   question: backdate the row to a fixed sentinel
   (`UPDATE … SET updated_at = '2001-01-01T00:00:00.000Z'`) and assert the
   sentinel survives, so the mutation fails by 25 years instead of a clock tick.
   Mutate each guard **independently** — two guards removed together only prove
   that at least one matters.

Also: extracting a route-private predicate into a small exported helper (e.g. `connectorRemoveState`) is a legitimate way to make gating logic testable, and is better factoring on its own merits. Flag it as a production change when reporting.

# Brief 4 — Prod follow-ups left open on 2026-08-15 (mostly READ-ONLY diagnosis)

> Each item is independent. Do them in any order. Three are diagnosis-only; two
> imply a small PR. Nothing here is urgent — none is breaking prod right now.
> **All prod SDK calls MUST pass `-c prod`** (see item 2 for why).

## 1. Connection 385 carries DUPLICATE active feed rows
`lobu-team/github-app-install` (connection 385) has two active `commits` feeds
(ids 363, 364) and two active `pull_requests` feeds (347, 354), all
`status: active`, `kind: collected`, all syncing successfully. So every sync
runs twice and ingests the same origin ids twice.

- Dedupe should make this harmless (events key on `origin_id` scoped to
  connection/source), but it doubles API quota and sync cost.
- Find out **how** duplicates were created — that is the real bug. A feed
  create path that does not upsert on `(connection_id, feed_key)` would
  reproduce this on every connector.
- Read-only first: `client.feeds.list({ connection_id: 385 })`, then compare
  `created_at` and config of each pair. Do NOT delete a feed without surfacing
  the pair and getting explicit confirmation.

## 2. The `lobu` CLI active context is `prodma-dev` (localhost:9455)
A dispatched agent switched it mid-session. Symptom is a confusing
`json.decoder.JSONDecodeError` from `lobu call`; the real cause only shows in raw
output as `MCP fetch failed … Tried: http://localhost:9455/...`.

**The fix is `lobu link`, not flipping the global context.** `apply`, `agent`,
`memory`, `connector`, and `org` accept NO `--context` flag (verified at
subcommand level too) and silently use whatever is active — `lobu apply` is the
sharp edge, since it would deploy to the wrong runtime with no way to pin inline.
`lobu link` binds a directory to a (context, org) pair in `.lobu/project.json`.

Do this per active worktree. See
`memory/reference_lobu_cli_context_flag_coverage.md`.

## 3. `syncGithubConnectionAcl` early-returns on zero repos without clearing
`packages/server/src/authz/github-acl-sync.ts` — when `repos.length === 0` it
returns `{ ok: true }` BEFORE `buildAccessGraph` and BEFORE
`clearConnectionAclError`. So a connection that previously failed ACL sync and
then legitimately drops to zero repos keeps its `acl: …` error_message forever,
and its `authz_source_acl_state` is never refreshed.

Introduced by PR #2788 (which added the persisted reason). Low likelihood, real.
Decide: clear the error on the zero-repo path, or treat zero repos as
not-graphed. **Confirm the intended semantics before writing code** — fail-closed
behavior on a security gate is involved.

## 4. Prod HTTP logs appear to contain `x-slack-signature`
Carried over from the #2771 work. The header is NOT logged from application
source on `origin/main` (only a comment mentions it), so this is almost certainly
the **ingress access log**, not `packages/server`. Fix at that layer; do not hunt
in the server package. Verify before acting — a secret in logs is worth
confirming rather than assuming.

## 5. An unscoped `slack-acl-sync failed` log carries no connection id
Same origin. Makes the failure unattributable in prod. One-line fix, but find
every sibling log in that file rather than just the one (fix the class).

Round 2 is addressed. Both findings were real, and one of them was me overruling the reviewer incorrectly.

**The blocker — genuine race, now fixed and proven.** `clearConnectionAclError` could observe `fresh`, block behind a committing failure, and then erase it — because under READ COMMITTED, re-checking a blocked row does **not** re-run the `EXISTS` subquery against the newer snapshot. Outcome would be `freshness_state='failed'` with no reason: exactly the blindness this PR exists to remove.

Fix: an unconditional `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` on the live connections row first, in **both** writers. That forces the freshness read into a statement beginning after the failure commits. It also closes the second half of the finding — my `IS DISTINCT FROM` guard meant a repeated identical failure took *no* row lock at all.

The regression test reproduces it precisely. Mutating the lock back out gives `expected null to be 'acl: newer failure'` — the exact corruption, so the test isn't vacuous.

**The whitespace churn — I was wrong to keep it.** My "reverting would turn format-lint red" claim came from running `biome check` without the repo's `--config-path config/biome.config.json`. With the real config, `bun run format:check` exits **0 both ways** — `access-graph.ts` is in biome's ignore list. So the churn was never load-bearing. Reverted:

**`which lobu` → `~/.bun/bin/lobu` was **13.4.0** on 2026-08-15, while
`prodma-demo` pinned `@lobu/cli ^14.22.0` (also the latest published).** Running
`lobu` from inside a project directory silently uses the GLOBAL one — bun does
not shim `node_modules/.bin` onto PATH the way `npm run` does.

## The symptom, which does not name the cause
```
PATCH /api/<org>/agents/<agent>/config failed: This server no longer accepts
"installedProviders". The agent's model configuration is now a single ordered
"models" list of explicit "<provider>/<model>" refs. Upgrade your client.
```
Nothing points at PATH. The fix is not to edit `lobu.config.ts` — the old CLI
serializes the config into the retired wire shape.

**Always use `./node_modules/.bin/lobu` inside a project** (or
`bunx @lobu/cli@latest`). Check with `lobu --version` vs
`./node_modules/.bin/lobu --version` before blaming config.

The stale CLI is not always loud: `context list`, `org create`, and
`apply --dry-run` all ran fine on 13.4.0. The dry-run plan even DIFFERED between
versions (48 create/0 update on 13.4.0 vs 46 create/1 update/1 noop on 14.22.0),
so a plan produced by the wrong CLI is not evidence of what a correct apply does.

## Related mechanics confirmed the same day
- `lobu apply` needs `--yes` when stdin is not a TTY.
- `lobu org create <slug>` does NOT create anything server-side — it only opens
  `https://app.lobu.ai/orgs/new?slug=…&name=…` in a browser for a human to
  complete. Pass the display name yourself; the CLI sends `name=<slug>`.
- `client.entitySchema.listTypes()` (NOT `client.entityTypes`) lists types, takes
  NO `scope` argument, and returns the org's own types PLUS public schemas — so
  filter on `organization_id` before counting or you will double-count.

## Executive verdict

Lobu can already provide a useful, schema-driven operational workspace around Prodma: typed current-state entities, relationships, editable document-line arrays, entity pickers, date controls, Behaviors, approvals, derived SQL, and point-in-time event metrics. It is **not yet a credible replacement for a manufacturing ERP of record**.

The decisive shortfall is not screen count. It is that Lobu does not yet have one non-bypassable, transaction-bound place where every entity and relationship mutation can enforce document state, accounting-period rules, statutory numbering, authorization, and durable audit. On current `origin/main`, the entity write path has **22 distinct raw INSERT/UPDATE bypass sites across nine runtime categories**, not the six categories shown on the old program board. Four additional hard-delete cleanup sites also sit outside canonical CRUD.

The honest positioning is therefore:

- **Credible now:** integration/context layer, configurable operational records, human-reviewed automation, and a PoC vertical slice.
- **Not credible now:** Turkish statutory books and documents, controlled posting, period close, gapless legal numbering, statutory-grade history, human row/field authorization, and reconciled ERP aggregates.
- **Potentially credible after platform work:** a narrow ERP vertical on Lobu, provided the shared persistence/enforcement layer is built first and statutory content is treated as a maintained product, not as prompts or one-off connector code.
- **Structurally conditional:** the locked “header plus lines in one JSONB metadata array” choice is good for one-row atomicity, but cannot also provide native line-level foreign keys, uniqueness, and relational constraints. If those database guarantees are required, that model choice must change or be backed by a stronger transactional projection.

=== gap 3 (lifecycle/transitions) ===
### 3. Document lifecycle, period close, legal numbering, and reversal semantics are absent

- **Severity:** P0 — accounting-control blocker.
- **Classification:** **Not built; cannot be represented safely as ordinary mutable metadata or prompt instructions.** Closeable after Gap 2.
- **Why it matters:** Draft, issued, posted, cancelled, reversed, and closed-period states are not labels. They determine whether stock, tax, receivables, GL entries, external documents, and numbers exist and whether later edits are legal.
- **Current evidence:** entity hooks support only `beforeCreate`, `afterCreate`, and `beforeDelete`, can be skipped, and have only a `$member` registration (`packages/server/src/utils/entity-hooks.ts:1-56`). Fresh root and pinned-UI searches found no `x-transitions`/transition rule primitive and no accounting-period-close primitive. Fresh exact numbering searches for the discarded implementation vocabulary returned no match in root or pinned UI. The ordinary update API accepts a metadata patch without a transition operation (`packages/core/src/contracts/tools/manage-entity.ts:14-54,182-187`).
- **Numbering correction:** there is no current code that “allocates too early.” The missing capability should eventually allocate a legal number on the first successful `draft → issued` transition, inside that same transaction, preserve gaps/voids according to the relevant document regime, and never recycle a committed number after rollback ambiguity.

export async function markConnectionAclFailed(
	organizationId: string,
	connectionId: string,
	reason: string,
): Promise<void> {
	const sql = getDb();
	const message = formatAclErrorMessage(reason);
	await sql.begin(async (tx) => {
		// Lock the live connection row FIRST and UNCONDITIONALLY. Two reasons:
		// (1) lock order is connections → ACL state, matching connection deletion
		// and fresh-state stamping, so a failing sync cannot deadlock against a
		// concurrent delete; (2) the message UPDATE below is conditional, so a
		// repeated identical failure would take no row lock at all and could
		// interleave with `clearConnectionAclError`.
		await tx`
      SELECT 1
      FROM connections
      WHERE organization_id = ${organizationId}
        AND deleted_at IS NULL
        AND ${tx.unsafe(aclConnectionIdSql())} = ${connectionId}
      FOR UPDATE
    `;
		await tx`
      UPDATE connections
      SET error_message = ${message}, updated_at = current_timestamp
      WHERE organization_id = ${organizationId}
        AND deleted_at IS NULL
        AND ${tx.unsafe(aclConnectionIdSql())} = ${connectionId}
        AND (
          error_message IS NULL
          OR left(error_message, ${ACL_ERROR_MESSAGE_PREFIX.length}) = ${ACL_ERROR_MESSAGE_PREFIX}
        )
        AND error_message IS DISTINCT FROM ${message}
    `;
		await tx`
      UPDATE authz_source_acl_state
      SET freshness_state = 'failed', updated_at = clock_timestamp()
      WHERE organization_id = ${organizationId}
        AND connection_id = ${connectionId}
    `;
	});
}

content.text:
Here's what `acme-usage` is, plus something more important that the query turned up.

**acme-usage is a demo connector, not a real integration.** "Acme" is the standard placeholder company name, and it lives in an org literally called `lobudemo` (`org_SAvKyHSn2Zk`). It has two feeds:

```
522 | accounts  | active | 16 failures | 256 items collected
523 | activity  | active | 16 failures | 512 items collected
```

It isn't in the codebase at all — `git grep` against `origin/main` finds nothing — so it's a DB-defined custom connector, built to give demos some plausible-looking account and usage data. The `items_collected` counts are the tell: it *used to work* and pulled 768 items, then its backing endpoint went away. Now it retries every 2 hours (`15 */2 * * *`, next runs 02:24 and 02:39 UTC) and fails with `fetch failed` each time. Pure noise — no customer impact, but it will keep polluting error rates forever.

**The more significant finding, and it corrects my earlier confidence:** 104 feeds are sitting on `worker_claim_timeout`, up to 69 consecutive failures each — 14 `tweets` feeds, `stargazers`, three Chrome feeds, `rss`, `reddit`.

They are *not* an active outage. 100 of them last synced **2026-07-18**, roughly a month ago. But here's the part worth your attention:

```
overdue: 0   future: 0   unscheduled: 104
```

All 104 have `next_run_at IS NULL` while still carrying `status='active'`. They're zombies — marked active, never scheduled, so they cannot recover on their own and nothing will retry them. Whatever cleared their schedule a month ago left them in a state the system won't heal.

So to answer your actual question: **prod is serving correctly** — pods ready, health 200, 17/19 syncs green, deployed SHA `078be4c03` confirmed. But the feed layer has 104 stuck feeds nobody is watching, and I should not have implied the sync picture was clean when I'd only looked at 25 minutes of logs.

Two corrections to things I said earlier:
- `consecutive_failures` is on **`feeds`**, not `connections`. My previous "connection 385: 1271 consecutive failures → 0" named the wrong table.
- The failure landscape was invisible from logs because these feeds stopped running a month ago — log-window checks structurally cannot see them.

Confidence:
- **What acme-usage is — 95.** Connector key, org, schedule, and item counts read directly from prod.
- **The 104 zombie feeds are real — 90.** Counts and null schedules are straight from the DB; I have not found *why* their schedules were cleared.
- **Prod serving health — 95**, unchanged and independently evidenced.

Next actions:
1. Want me to investigate what cleared `next_run_at` on those 104 feeds in July? That's the actual bug — an `active` feed with no schedule should be impossible.
2. Pause or repoint the two `acme-usage` demo feeds so they stop failing every 2 hours.
3. Consider whether `status='active' AND next_run_at IS NULL` deserves an alert — it's currently a silent failure mode.
4. I'll fix the prod-DB recipe memory (pod renamed to `lobu-db-prod-1`, `consecutive_failures` is on `feeds`, and `organization` uses camelCase `createdAt`).

Which is expected, and it's the gap itself: there's no relational import path, because connectors can't declare entity→entity edges yet. Every invoice→customer or line→product edge would need one SDK call per edge. So "up to date" is true for the schema and misleading for the import — nothing has been imported, and the mechanism to do it in bulk doesn't exist.

**On deleting — I did the two, and stopped on the 104. The condition you set doesn't hold for them.**

Those 104 feeds are not dead-and-unused. They have real history behind them:

| Org | Feeds | Items collected | Last sync |
|---|---|---|---|

| Lobu Community | 23 | 1,715,818 | 2026-07-18 |
| Lobu Team | 4 | 12,982 | 2026-07-18 |

That's ~6.8M collected items across four real orgs. They're not abandoned — they're **stalled**: `status='active'` with `next_run_at IS NULL`, so they stopped being scheduled a month ago and can't recover on their own. Deleting them would destroy working connector config and the only visible evidence of whatever broke in July. The fix is to restore their schedule, not remove them. I'd rather find out what cleared `next_run_at` first, since whatever did it could do it again.

The `acme-usage` pair genuinely does meet your bar — demo org (`lobudemo`, 1 member), dead endpoint, failing every 2 hours. - **acme-usage is safe to remove — 90.** Demo org, dead endpoint. Unverified: whether you use it in live demos.

10	
11	**`lobu apply` has no `--context` flag.** Neither do `agent`, `memory`,
12	`connector`, or `org` — including their subcommands (checked `agent list`,
13	`memory run`, `org show`, `connector run`: zero context flags, so the flag does
14	not live one level down). They silently operate on whatever context is active.
15	
16	Verified empirically 2026-08-15 against the installed CLI:
17	
18	| Accepts `-c/--context` | Does NOT |
19	|---|---|
20	| `call`, `status`, `whoami`, `chat`, `token`, `link`, `login`/`logout` | `apply`, `agent`, `memory`, `connector`, `org` |
21	
22	## Why it bites
23	A dispatched agent can switch the global context (one switched it to
24	`prodma-dev` → `localhost:9455` mid-session). Every `lobu call` afterwards fails
25	with a confusing `json.decoder.JSONDecodeError`, whose real cause only shows in
26	raw output: `MCP fetch failed … Tried: http://localhost:9455/api/<org>/<tool>`.
27	Pin with `-c prod` to confirm that diagnosis.
28	
29	The sharp edge is `apply`: it deploys `lobu.config.ts` to the active context with
30	no way to pin inline, so a stale context sends a prod-intended apply to localhost
31	or vice versa. Same exposure on `agent delete`.
32	
33	## The fix is `lobu link`, not flipping the global context
34	`lobu link` binds a directory to a (context, org) pair in `.lobu/project.json`,
35	so each checkout operates against the right runtime regardless of the global
36	active context. That is what makes the flagless commands safe. Flipping the
37	global context back and forth just relocates the race.
38	
39	## Unrelated: codex's lobu MCP is NOT affected by the CLI context
40	`~/.codex/config.toml` hardcodes `mcp_servers.lobu = https://app.lobu.ai/mcp`
41	(prod) and `mcp_servers.lobu-local` = a tailscale URL. A codex
42	`MCP startup incomplete (failed: lobu, lobu-local)` is therefore NOT context
43	drift — prod `/mcp` correctly returns 401 with a well-formed RFC 9728
44	`www-authenticate: Bearer resource_metadata=… scope="mcp:read mcp:write"`
45	challenge (codex simply holds no token), and `lobu-local` is unreachable when the
46	local stack is not running. Do not chase this as a Lobu defect.
47

`memory` and `agent` — it was produced by a grep whose ERE pattern (`"\-\-context"`)
silently matched nothing. Re-verified one command at a time against CLI 14.22.0:

| Accepts `-c/--context` | Does NOT |
|---|---|
| `call`, `status`, `whoami`, `chat`, `token`, `link`, `login`/`logout`, **`memory exec`**, **`memory run`**, **`memory seed`**, **`agent list`** | **`apply`**, `org show` |

So the only genuinely flagless sharp edge is **`apply`**. Lesson worth more than the
table: a `grep -c` that returns 0 for EVERY row is a broken pattern, not a finding —
`\-` is undefined in ERE. Verify a negative sweep against one known-positive case.

## `apply` now has a project-link GUARD (this is the real mechanism)
`lobu apply --help` shows:
`--force   Bypass the project-link guard if context/org don't match`

So once a directory is linked, `apply` REFUSES to run against a mismatched
context/org instead of silently targeting the active one. `lobu link` is not just
a convenience — it arms the guard. An unlinked directory has no guard at all,
which is how a prod-intended apply reaches localhost.

**acme-usage is deleted** — `UPDATE 2`, both feeds now `paused` and tombstoned, schedule cleared. They'll stop failing every 2 hours. The 768 already-collected items are untouched, and it's reversible.

**Why prod data isn't up to date**

It's not that the data went stale — it was **never written to prod at all**. The seed scripts ran against a local context. There's a `prodma-dev` context at `localhost:9455` sitting right there in your context list, and `~/Code/prodma-demo` had **no `.lobu/project.json`**, so nothing bound the directory to prod. Whatever context happened to be active won.

I've fixed the root cause:

```json
{ "context": "prod", "org": "prodma-erp", "linkedAt": "2026-08-15T20:56:01.752Z" }
```

That matters more than it looks. `lobu apply` has a `--force` flag described as *"Bypass the project-link guard if context/org don't match"* — meaning once a directory is linked, apply **refuses** to run against the wrong runtime. Unlinked, there was no guard at all. That was the actual bug, and it's now armed.

**The best way to load the data**

Your repo already has the right scripts; they just need to run against prod, in this order:

1. `seed-full.ts` — 25 Turkish manufacturing customers + products. Idempotent (skips existing names).
2. `seed-chain.ts` — builds Teklif → Fatura → Tahsilat as a real chain. This supersedes `seed-docs.ts`, which generated each document type independently so `invoice_from_quote` stayed empty. Use chain, not docs.
3. `backfill-links.ts` — **re-run until `remaining` is 0.** The script sandbox caps at 200 SDK calls per run, so it deliberately writes ~180 edges at a time.

That 200-call cap is your gap analysis in miniature: one call per entity, one per edge, no bulk path.

**I'm blocked on running them.** The permission classifier refused the seed execution twice. Since it's your call, here are the exact commands — run each with `!` in the prompt:

```
! cd ~/Code/prodma-demo && ./node_modules/.bin/lobu memory exec "$(cat scripts/seed-full.ts)" --org prodma-erp
! cd ~/Code/prodma-demo && ./node_modules/.bin/lobu memory exec "$(cat scripts/seed-chain.ts)" --org prodma-erp
! cd ~/Code/prodma-demo && ./node_modules/.bin/lobu memory exec "$(cat scripts/backfill-links.ts)" --org prodma-erp
```

Use `./node_modules/.bin/lobu`, not bare `lobu` — the global one is 13.4.0 and will fail on `installedProviders`.

Two corrections to things I told you earlier:
- `lobu memory exec/run/seed` and `agent list` **do** accept `--context`. My earlier sweep said they didn't; it was a `grep -c` with a malformed `\-\-context` pattern that matched nothing on every row. A negative result on every single row should have tipped me off. `apply` is the genuine exception.
- The `--org prodma-erp` flag alone was never sufficient protection, since it names the org but not the runtime.

Confidence:
- **acme-usage removed — 100.** Before/after rows confirmed.
- **Diagnosis of the empty prod data — 85.** The missing link file and the local `prodma-dev` context are hard facts; I did not connect to `:9455` to confirm the data actually landed there.
- **Seed sequence is correct — 80.** Read from the scripts' own headers; I have not executed them end to end.

Next actions:
1. Run the three commands above; paste me the output and I'll verify the entity counts in prod.
2. If you'd rather I run them, add a Bash permission rule for `lobu memory exec`.
3. Worth confirming whether `prodma-dev` at `:9455` holds the old seed — if so, that's your proof of where it went, and it can be retired.

feat(demo): make the Teklif -> Siparis -> Fatura -> Tahsilat chain traversable

The chain could not be expressed. `order_from_quote` covered the first hop and
`payment_invoice` the last, but nothing joined the middle, and there was no
invoice->product edge while quote and order both had one. seed-chain.ts targeted
`document_product` and `invoice_from_quote`, neither of which exists.

Adds `invoice_from_order` and `invoice_product`, declares `order_id` on invoice,
and routes the seeder through the order.

Three schema/write-path behaviours the seeder now has to work around:
- a declared `default` does NOT satisfy a required field on create, so
  `cari_type` and `document_type` are stamped explicitly
- `entities.update` validates the PATCH, not the merged result, so a status-only
  transition is rejected for missing `customer_id`; every required field is
  resent on each transition
- a soft-deleted entity still holds its name, so a re-run after a delete
  collides — hence the SERIES constant

Result in the prodma-erp org: 40 quotes, 24 orders, 14 invoices, 2 payments,
345 edges, zero errors.
EOF
)"

---
name: reference_entity_write_path_gaps_found_seeding_prod
description: "Three entity write-path behaviours proven against PROD while seeding the Prodma ERP demo — declared defaults do not satisfy required, update validates the patch not the merge, and a soft-deleted entity still holds its name"
metadata:
  node_type: memory
  type: reference
---

Found 2026-08-15 seeding the `prodma-erp` prod org. All three are **confirmed
against prod**, not inferred — each one failed a real `entities.create` /
`entities.update` call and the fix was verified by a subsequent green run.

## 1. A declared `default` does NOT satisfy a `required` field on create
`customer.cari_type` and `invoice.document_type` both declare `default:` in the
schema and both appear in `required:`. Creating without them fails:

```
Metadata validation failed: missing required field: cari_type
Metadata validation failed: missing required field: document_type
```

So the write path validates the **submitted payload**, not the payload merged
with schema defaults. A field cannot be both `required` and usefully defaulted —
every caller must stamp it. Worth deciding whether that is intended, because the
schema reads as though the default covers it.

## 2. `entities.update` validates the PATCH, not the merged result
Confirms [[reference_entity_update_validates_the_patch_not_the_merge]] in prod.
A status-only transition on an invoice:

```js
client.entities.update({ entity_id, metadata: { status: "issued" } })
// -> Metadata validation failed: missing required field: customer_id
```

The stored row HAS `customer_id`. The patch does not, so it is rejected. Every
transition must resend every required field. Consequence for the ERP work: a
state machine over a type with required fields cannot be driven by a minimal
patch, which is exactly what a transition hook would want to emit.

## 3. A soft-deleted entity still holds its name
`entities.delete` tombstones (`deleted_at`), but the name-uniqueness constraint
still counts the tombstone. Re-creating the same name afterwards fails with
`Entity already exists with this name/domain`. So delete-then-reseed does NOT
work; the seeder needs a fresh document series instead. Relevant to any
idempotent import that assumes delete frees the key.

## What this cost
Four failed seeding runs, each surfacing exactly one of these. None is visible
from the schema alone.

Related: [[project_prodma_demo_repo_and_prod_org]] ·
[[project_entity_write_path_has_no_identity_contract]] ·
[[project_prodma_boundary_is_erp_of_record]]

|---|---|

**Entity types — verified live just now:**

```
own entity types          15   (your 14 + the built-in $member)
relationship types        34   (32 + the 2 I added today)
visible incl. public      61   (org types + public schemas — don't count these)

The 14: `bom`, `cheque`, `customer`, `invoice`, `journal-entry`, `ledger-account`, `order`, `payment`, `price-list`, `product`, `quote`, `stock-movement`, `warehouse`, `work-order`.

That's 14 types against Prodma's 422 tables, which is the deliberate compression from the gap analysis: one type per distinct table *cluster*, with in-table discriminators kept as fields rather than types — supplier/bank/employee are `cari_type` values on `customer`, not separate types; alış/satış is a `direction` on `order`.

One incidental finding: `entity_types` is **not** in the SDK sandbox's queryable allowlist (only 15 tables are, including `entity_relationship_types` but not `entity_types`), so type counts have to come from `client.entitySchema.listTypes()` — and that returns public schemas too, which is why the naive count says 61.

- **No real Prodma data exists in the dump — 90.** I searched for the obvious data-file extensions at depth 3; a deeper or differently-named export could exist.
- **Type counts — 98.** Read live from prod and filtered on `organization_id`.

result.output:
Root cause, one sentence: **Lobu's entity store is a KNOWLEDGE store (current state, org-scoped, mutable); an ERP needs a LEDGER (historical, row-scoped, deterministic, immutable).** Four consequences:
1. **No history.** `manage_entity` writes NO event and NO audit row (grep-verified). `entity_type_audit` audits the SCHEMA only. No entity field-version table exists. `asOf` read mode is DECLARED but raises NotImplemented. No period concept ⇒ backdated writes have nothing to invalidate.
2. **No immutability.** No frozen/posted concept, no `beforeUpdate` hook, no declarative state machine (JSON Schema can't express transitions). Status is a plain metadata string.
3. **No row-level scope.** Reads scoped by org+role+column+table (`validateAndScopeQuery` — careful, NOT a bypass; an agent claimed "read-seam bypass", overstated), but never per-row. Two humans in one org always see identical rows.
4. **No transaction boundary for org code.** Sandbox = read-only scoped SQL, no write handle; connectors get no DB handle (worker-credentials invariant). An atomic multi-write path EXISTS (Behavior declared-output) but is data-in/no-code.
Plus the sleeper: **aggregates don't scale** — write-time materialization is hand-authored per number; runtime-definable aggregates are read-time SQL that the invariant forbids. "No without a developer per number."

**★ KEY DESIGN INSIGHT — store document lines as a metadata ARRAY, not child entities.** Header+lines then = ONE `entities` row = ONE write = **naturally atomic**. This dissolves gap 4, shrinks immutability to a single write-gate check, and reduces concurrency to a single-row lock. The data-model decision erases the architectural gap. Cost: line-level queries need a derived view (`backing_sql`). This is question S1 in the Turkish working doc and everything else hangs off it.

**Generated-UI ceiling is the ACTION vocabulary, not components.** TWO registries exist — `components` AND `actions` (`RendererAction`) — both caller-supplied, and **neither is passed at any call site**. A generated template can REFERENCE an action by name but cannot DEFINE one. Seed the verb list from Prodma's 170+ operation codes.

**Artifact is now a TURKISH working doc** with 8 numbered decisions (S1–S8) for the user to answer, the proposed 24 entity types, a concrete `fatura` JSON Schema, and the relationship graph.

**★★ ROUND 2 — the user challenged all 7 gaps and was RIGHT on 4. My "architectural gap" list was substantially WRONG; corrected against code.** Decisions locked: S1=A (lines in metadata), S2=A (rule engine in sandbox), S3=B (history for documents only), S4=A (posted doc frozen), S5=A (row-level via relationships), S6 OPEN, S7=A (`FiyatService` authoritative), S8=A (Teklif→Fatura chain).
1. **History — still absent, but SMALL not architectural.** `events` already has `created_by`/`entity_ids`/`occurred_at`/`supersedes_event_id` + GIN `idx_events_entity_ids`. The write path just never calls it. `manage_entity.ts:216` writes `watcher_reactions` ONLY when `args.behavior_source` is set (Behavior-sourced writes), and stores `{action,entity_type,name,entity_id}` — no field diff. Human edits record nothing.
2. **Freeze hook EXISTS — I was flat wrong.** `packages/server/src/authz/entity-mutation-gate.ts` is a registered interceptor pipeline in front of every user-facing entity write; outcomes allow/deny/defer, first deny wins, `registerMutationInterceptor()` at :186. Its own header says a new gate = ONE new file, zero core edits. **The only blocker: `entity-policy.ts:796` `if (args.principalKind === "user") return "allow";`** — same short-circuit at :883, :916, :976. So freeze binds AGENTS today, not humans.
3. **State machine = same lift as #2.** JSON Schema can't express old→new transitions in ANY draft (validates a doc in isolation) — no library fixes it. The interceptor sees both `current` and `proposed`, so declare transitions as `x-state-machine` in `metadata_schema` and interpret in the same file.
4. **Row-level authz via relationships is EXACTLY what Lobu already built.** `authz/access-graph.ts` writes `member_of` edges + reconciles leavers + stamps freshness; `authz/resource-visibility.ts` enforces membership at read time and FAILS CLOSED on a stale graph. **But it is wired to the `events` read seam, not `entities`.** Also `entity_approval_policies.entity_id` targets ONE entity (write-side, non-human only) and `entities.field_controls` is per-row-per-field.
5. **Lobu is NOT event-sourced for entities** — `entities` is mutated in place. `updateEntity` does the whole read-modify-write in one `sql.begin` (entity-management.ts:616) with `FOR UPDATE` (:623). Behavior declared-output commits N entities in the window tx (promote-keyed-entities.ts:438, "atomic contract"). Sandbox `client.query` forces `SET TRANSACTION READ ONLY` (client-sdk.ts:263). After S1+S2 only the POSTING step needs >1 row ⇒ outbox/saga, not event sourcing.
6. **Aggregates = the ONE surviving architectural gap.** Two read-time paths, no materialization anywhere (**zero `CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW` in all migrations**): (a) `entity_types.backing_sql` — derived types are live SQL views over our own tables, runtime-definable, but recompute every read; (b) `entity_types.metrics_config` + `metrics/compiler.ts` — a real declared semantic layer, **but compiles `FROM events` ONLY**, joins entities by `eventSet.by:"alias"` text matching, and cross-entity joins / `window`/`link` / `raw`/`asOf` are explicitly NotImplemented. So "SUM of this customer's invoices" is INEXPRESSIBLE — invoices are entities, not events. Real fix = open the existing metric compiler to an entity source + materialize. Denormalized-field route's trap: one missed write path silently corrupts the number (this is why Prodma has "accounting repair tool" screens).
7. **Concurrency — half already solved.** `FOR UPDATE` serializes same-entity writes; `field_controls` gives a human per-field ownership that a later agent write cannot overwrite (queues an approval). Missing is HUMAN-vs-HUMAN: no version check, second write silently wins — and with S1=A that clobbers the whole line array. Fix = optimistic lock (~10 lines inside the tx that already holds the row lock; `updated_at` exists).
**Net: 7 architectural gaps → 1.** The question is no longer "can Lobu carry an ERP" but "what happens when Lobu's existing gate/authz/metric layers are pointed at entities too" — all three are already written, just aimed at other data.
Also confirmed blocking-but-small: `dynamic-schema-form.tsx` renders no date, no datetime, no entity-lookup — every ERP screen needs all three.

Found them, and one of these matters more than the entity-type question.

**The Excels are real Prodma exports — but they're system metadata, not business data.**

`M_MENU (1).xlsx` has 7 sheets:

| Sheet | Rows | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| `M_MENU` | 533 | the menu tree / 453 screens |
| `M_ALANLAR` | 0 | field definitions — empty |
| `M_ALAN_TIP` | 10 | field types |
| `YETKI` | 201 | **permissions** |
| `YETKI_ISLEM_TANITIM` | 201 | **permission operation definitions** |
| `YETKI_ISLEMLER` | 201 | **permission operations** |
| `M_ALAN_GOSTERILEN` | 5 | displayed fields |

So they still can't seed customers or invoices — there's no CARI/STOK/FATURA data anywhere. My synthetic seed stands for now.

**But the three YETKI sheets are the evidence the design doc said it was missing.** That doc explicitly recorded: it was reading Prodma's permission model from how the WinForms code hides fields, called that an assumption, and said *"the truncated permission sheets are the evidence I'd have used to confirm it, and I'm proceeding without them by decision."* It even named the tell — if a salesperson can see another's accounts, the model is row-level and the deferred row-level-read design comes back. Those sheets are now in hand at 201 rows each, so that assumption is checkable instead of deferred. Given you've chosen ERP-of-record, an authz model that turns out to be row-level would be a significant re-rank.

**On entity types — yes, you're right, and we're short.**

The original proposal was **24**. We shipped **14** (plus the built-in `$member`), and 34 relationship types. So roughly 10 were dropped.

Cross-referencing the real menu's module structure against our 14, the concretely missing domains are:

| Prodma module | Forms | Status |
|---|---|---|
| `SabitKiymet` (fixed assets) | 5 | **missing** |
| `Mahsup` (offset/settlement) | 2 | **missing** |
| `MasrafYeri` (cost center) | 1 | **missing** |
| `Satis`, `Siparis`, `Teklif`, `Cek`, `Recete`, `AmbarFisleri`, `Muhasebe`, `Mrp` | 176 | covered |
| `AlisSatis` (purchase/sales) | 32 | partly — folded into `order.direction` |
| `Ortak` (shared) | 12 | unclear |

I can name those three with confidence because they map to whole modules with no corresponding type. The remaining ~7 I can't reconstruct — the 24-item list lived in an earlier version of the Turkish working doc, and the artifact I fetched (`b65a24ee`) is the later "five spikes" revision, which doesn't enumerate them. There are 16 other artifacts in my memory; the list is likely in one of them.

- **Excels are Prodma system metadata, not business data — 95.** Sheet names and row counts read directly.
- **24 proposed vs 14 shipped — 85.** The "24" comes from my own memory note, not from a document I re-read today.
- **The three named missing modules — 90.** Grounded in the menu export; `Ortak` I genuinely can't classify.

## Executive verdict

Lobu can already provide a useful, schema-driven operational workspace around Prodma: typed current-state entities, relationships, editable document-line arrays, entity pickers, date controls, Behaviors, approvals, derived SQL, and point-in-time event metrics. It is **not yet a credible replacement for a manufacturing ERP of record**.

The decisive shortfall is not screen count. It is that Lobu does not yet have one non-bypassable, transaction-bound place where every entity and relationship mutation can enforce document state, accounting-period rules, statutory numbering, authorization, and durable audit. On current `origin/main`, the entity write path has **22 distinct raw INSERT/UPDATE bypass sites across nine runtime categories**, not the six categories shown on the old program board. Four additional hard-delete cleanup sites also sit outside canonical CRUD.

The honest positioning is therefore:

- **Credible now:** integration/context layer, configurable operational records, human-reviewed automation, and a PoC vertical slice.
- **Not credible now:** Turkish statutory books and documents, controlled posting, period close, gapless legal numbering, statutory-grade history, human row/field authorization, and reconciled ERP aggregates.
- **Potentially credible after platform work:** a narrow ERP vertical on Lobu, provided the shared persistence/enforcement layer is built first and statutory content is treated as a maintained product, not as prompts or one-off connector code.
- **Structurally conditional:** the locked “header plus lines in one JSONB metadata array” choice is good for one-row atomicity, but cannot also provide native line-level foreign keys, uniqueness, and relational constraints. Planning — decisions owed, gaps ranked, order fixed

Prodma Build Order

The boundary question is answered, so the register can finally be ranked rather than hedged. One gap closed on new evidence, one is a product problem rather than a platform one, and everything else queues behind a single piece of plumbing.

Boundary ERP of record Prod org prodma-erp · 17 types · 34 edges Gaps 12 ranked Decisions owed 5

Section 01

What changed, and what it costs

You chose ERP of record over a workspace around Prodma. That single answer is the ranking key: it makes the write funnel mandatory rather than optional, and it puts four gaps strictly behind it. Nothing in steps 3–6 of the build order can start before it.

Two things moved since the register was written, both from evidence rather than opinion.

Closed on evidence Row-level authzProdma's YETKI tables are 5 roles × 101 screens with no row predicate. Screen and operation grain, exactly as assumed.
Reclassified Statutory contentGap 1 is a product and vendor problem, not platform engineering. It runs in parallel, not in the queue.
Built and verified Demo org17 entity types, 34 relationships, 145 documents, 413 edges. The document chain traverses end to end.
New findings Write pathThree behaviours proven in prod that any transition design has to survive. Section 04.

The authz find is worth dwelling on. The earlier design doc flagged its own permission assumption as unverified and named the falsifying test — if one salesperson can see another's accounts, the model is row-level and a deferred design comes back. The permission sheets that would settle it have now turned up in the M_MENU export: three YETKI tables, 201 rows each, mapping roles to screens to operation flags. There is no row predicate column anywhere in them. The assumption held, so Gap 5 drops from P0 to P2 and the row-level read design stays closed.

Section 02

Decisions we owe

These are not engineering unknowns — they are calls only you or Prodma's owner can make, and each one changes what gets built. They are listed by how much downstream work they unblock, not by urgency.

D1

Does a document line need database-enforced integrity?

Lines currently live as a JSONB array on the document — one row, naturally atomic, which is why the model was chosen. The cost is that Postgres cannot enforce a line's foreign key, uniqueness, or sum. Every such rule has to be enforced in application code instead.

Why it matters: this is the only decision that can turn a P1 into a P0. If line-level database guarantees are non-negotiable, the one-row model has to change, and that reshapes the funnel, the audit journal and the aggregates all at once. Answer this before Step 1, not after.

D2

Where does the statutory boundary sit?

Turkish statutory books, e-Fatura/GİB integration, and the legal chart of accounts are absent and are not something to derive from the source code. This needs the owner and their accountant, plus a decision on which GİB integrator to contract.

Why it matters: it is a P0 legal go-live blocker but it is parallelisable — it is content and vendor work, not platform engineering. Starting it now costs nothing from the build queue and it has the longest external lead time of anything here.

D3

Can we get a real Prodma data export?

What we have is application source plus a menu and permission export. There is no CARI, STOK or FATURA data anywhere in it, so the demo org is seeded with synthetic Turkish manufacturer data. A SQL Server export of even three tables would change that.

Why it matters: it decides whether the demo is credible to a domain expert, and it is the only way to validate the entity model against real cardinality and real edge cases rather than against a generator.

D4

Which of the original 24 entity types do we actually want?

The first proposal had 24 types. The org shipped with 14. Three obvious omissions have just been added — fixed-asset, cost-center and offset, each a whole Prodma module with its own forms — taking it to 17.

Why it matters: the remaining seven were dropped without a recorded rationale, so we cannot tell deliberate compression from oversight. Worth reconstructing the original list before modelling anything else on top.

D5

Is pre-printed form output a requirement?

Deterministic PDF and archive output, and whether documents must align to pre-printed stationery, materially change the printing work in Gap 11.

Why it matters: low effort to answer, and it is the difference between a reporting feature and a pixel-exact layout engine. Cheap to ask, expensive to guess wrong.

Section 03

The build order

This sequence is genuinely sequential — that is why it is numbered. Each step is blocked by the one above it, and the reason is the same throughout: they all need one transaction-bound place to stand.

  1. The write funnel — to zero bypasses

    P0 · blocks 2–5

    ~22 raw INSERT/UPDATE sites across 9 categories, plus 4 hard-delete sites outside canonical CRUD. One policy-neutral persistence module that always accepts the caller's open transaction.

  2. Approval and invariant separation

    P0

    Untangle "needs a human to approve" from "is structurally illegal". They are folded together in the current gate and only one of them belongs in the funnel.

  3. Merge and unmerge as first-class operations

    P1

    Unmerge already exists at entity-merge.ts:464. Both need to route through the funnel without regressing agent auto-merge.

  4. The entity write hook

    P0 · gated

    Stays disabled until step 1 reports zero bypasses. This is the seam a transition can use to cause a write, not merely refuse one — posting an invoice emitting its journal entry in the same commit.

  5. Lifecycle, period close, numbering, reversal

    P0

    Versioned org-owned transition rules, transaction-local period checks, idempotent issue/post/reverse, and a gapless numbering service. Numbering is absent from main — it exists only on a discarded branch.

  6. Statutory audit journal

    P0

    Immutable operation journal in the same transaction as every protected mutation, covering create, delete, link, unlink, merge, import and approval — most of which record nothing today.

The trap this ordering exists to avoid. Three previous branches were discarded for putting ERP vocabulary inside packages/server — transition freeze, period close, gapless numbering. Whatever gets built at steps 4–6 must be a generic platform capability an ERP is built on, never ERP concepts in the platform. There is no x-transitions, x-period-close or x-numbering anywhere in main, and that is the correct state.

Section 04

Three write-path behaviours to design around

Found while seeding the prod org. Each one broke a run, each was fixed and re-verified, and none is visible from the schema alone. They constrain the transition design directly.

BehaviourWhat happensConsequence for the plan
A declared default does not satisfy required Create fails with missing required field even though the schema declares a default for it. A field cannot be both required and usefully defaulted. Every caller must stamp it — including any generated importer.
Update validates the patch, not the merge {status:"issued"} is rejected for a missing customer_id the stored row already has. Directly blocks the state machine. A transition cannot emit a minimal patch, which is exactly what a transition hook would want to send.
A soft-deleted entity still holds its name Delete then re-create the same name fails with Entity already exists. Delete does not free the key, so any idempotent import that assumes it does will stall on the second run.

Section 05

The register, re-ranked

Twelve gaps, re-ordered under the ERP-of-record reading. Severity is from the register; the rank and the blocking relationships are what changed.

#GapSevStatus / blocked by
2Non-bypassable transaction-bound write funnelP0The keystone. Blocks 3, 4, 7, 9.
3Lifecycle, period close, numbering, reversalP0Blocked by 2. Numbering absent from main.
4Statutory audit trailP0Blocked by 2.
1Turkish statutory and accounting productP0Parallel — vendor and content work. Start now (D2).
6One-row document model vs line integrityP1Conditional — becomes P0 if D1 says yes.
7Governed aggregates and reconciliationP1Blocked by 2. "SUM of this customer's invoices" is inexpressible today.
8Connector/sandbox unsuitable for bulk relational loadP1Sandbox caps at 200 SDK calls; one call per entity and per edge.
9Human-vs-human silent overwriteP1Blocked by 2. Worst case clobbers a whole line array.
10Behaviors are not a durable posting sagaP1Needed for posting side effects, not ordinary automation.
11Operator UX and deterministic document outputP1Scope depends on D5.
12Vertical config not reproducible for all keysP2Underscore keys break apply. Deployment reliability only.
5Human row/field authorization on entity readsClosedDowngraded on YETKI evidence. No row predicate in Prodma's model.

Section 06

What is already true

Worth stating plainly, because the register is a list of what is missing and reads bleaker than the position actually is.

  • The mutation gate exists — a registered interceptor pipeline in front of every user-facing entity write. A new gate is one new file, zero core edits. Its only blocker is a short-circuit that returns allow for human principals.
  • The authz graph exists and fails closed on staleness — it is simply wired to the events read seam rather than entities.
  • The metric compiler exists as a real declared semantic layer. It compiles FROM events only, which is why entity aggregates are inexpressible — the fix is to open an existing compiler to a new source, not to build one.
  • The generic form renders documents. Line-item grids, linked-entity pickers and date controls all shipped; the keystone UI gap every other UI objection hung off is closed.
  • The demo org works end to end — 40 quotes, 24 orders, 14 invoices, 6 payments, and every payment traverses back to its customer through the full chain.

The recurring pattern across every round of this analysis is that the primitives are present but aimed at different data, or sit at a different grain than an ERP developer expects. That is a materially better position than absence — and it is why the funnel is worth doing first rather than working around.

Sources: ranked gap register (12 entries) · M_MENU export, 7 sheets including three YETKI permission tables · live prodma-erp prod org · origin/main absence checks. Severity ratings are the register's; ranking and blocking relationships are derived from the ERP-of-record decision.

**D3 done — prod is seeded.** 238 entities across 10 populated types, 473 edges, zero errors. New: 12 fixed assets, 9 cost centers, 8 offsets, 60 stock movements with `movement_product` edges. Commit `5bc8eb0`, pushed.

**D5 — yes, you're right, and reaction scripts are genuinely the correct tool there.** Document output is inherently post-hoc: nothing about generating a PDF needs to happen inside the write transaction. Deterministic reaction scripts handle it well. I'd only flag that "deterministic" has to mean no model in the rendering path, or two runs produce different invoices.

**D2 and D4 noted** — proper model with mock integrations, and cover what Prodma covers without mirroring it 1:1.

## On the architecture — you're right about half of it, and the half you're wrong about is load-bearing

I verified rather than reasoned about this, because it's the decision everything hangs off.

**Reaction scripts cannot enforce.** Three findings from `origin/main`:

1. Reactions are **post-commit**. The code says so in its own comment: `queue() runs AFTER the entity tx + change event so the approval ... is never rolled back with the edit`. `recordChangeEvent` fires outside the `sql.begin` block.
2. The sandbox forces `SET TRANSACTION READ ONLY` (`sandbox/client-sdk.ts:263`).
3. The mutation gate, by contrast, runs **inside** `sql.begin`, holding the row's `FOR UPDATE` lock (`entity-management.ts:696`, `sql: tx`).

So a reaction script sees a write that has already committed and is already visible, in a read-only sandbox, with no ability to roll it back. It can observe and compensate. It cannot refuse.

For an ERP of record that's the difference between "this invoice cannot be altered after posting" and "we noticed someone altered a posted invoice and tried to undo it." The second one isn't an accounting control.

**But your instinct is right about scope.** The mistake would be putting *workflow* in the write path. The split I'd argue for:

| | Where | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Invariants** — posted docs frozen, period closed, numbering gapless | Write path, in-transaction | Only place that can say no |
| **Consequences** — notify, report, reconcile, render PDF | Reaction scripts | Post-hoc by nature; your D5 case |
| **Autonomous work** — what the AI decides to do | Behaviors | Exactly what they're for |

And the gate is **not** overengineering: its own header says a new gate is one new file, zero core edits. The pipeline already exists. Its only blocker is a short-circuit returning `allow` for human principals — so today it binds agents but not people.

**The one genuinely hard case is Spike 5.** An interceptor can *refuse* a transition but cannot *cause* a write. Posting an invoice must emit its journal entry in the same commit — and a post-commit reaction gives you precisely "late, or never," because Behaviors are not a saga engine (no idempotency keys, no outbox, no compensation states). A posted invoice with no journal entry is a real books problem, not a retry problem. That's the one place I'd argue for an in-transaction hook regardless.

**D1 — you've actually already answered it.** "JSON arrays inside object could be pointing to high-level objects" is exactly what's running in prod now: lines carry `product_id` in the JSONB array *and* we materialize `invoice_product` / `order_product` / `movement_product` edges. Atomic one-row writes, traversable graph. The residual risk is that the two layers can drift, since nothing enforces that a line's `product_id` matches its edge — which is, again, a job for the funnel.

Confidence:
- **Reactions cannot enforce — 97.** Three independent code confirmations including an explicit comment.
- **Seeded prod state — 98.** Counts read back live.
- **The split I'm proposing — 85.** Sound on the mechanics; the Spike 5 boundary is a judgement call you may weigh differently.

Next actions:
1. Decide Spike 5 specifically: in-transaction hook for statutory side effects, or accept eventual consistency in the books. This is now the sharpest open question.
2. The funnel agent is still on Phase A — this split is exactly what its plan should be built against; want me to send it?
3. Removing the human-principal short-circuit is small and unblocks the gate binding people, not just agents.
4. I can update the build-order artifact with this architecture split once you've settled Spike 5.

The chosen design is that business rules are enforced by the write a Behavior performs, with autonomous work defined in Behaviors — rather than a large interceptor framework layered over everything. These are not engineering unknowns — they are calls only you or Prodma's owner can make, and each one changes what gets built. They are listed by how much downstream work they unblock, not by urgency.

D1

Does a document line need database-enforced integrity?

Lines currently live as a JSONB array on the document — one row, naturally atomic, which is why the model was chosen. The cost is that Postgres cannot enforce a line's foreign key, uniqueness, or sum. Every such rule has to be enforced in application code instead.

Why it matters: this is the only decision that can turn a P1 into a P0. If line-level database guarantees are non-negotiable, the one-row model has to change, and that reshapes the funnel, the audit journal and the aggregates all at once. Answer this before Step 1, not after.

D2

Where does the statutory boundary sit?

Turkish statutory books, e-Fatura/GİB integration, and the legal chart of accounts are absent and are not something to derive from the source code. This needs the owner and their accountant, plus a decision on which GİB integrator to contract.

Why it matters: it is a P0 legal go-live blocker but it is parallelisable — it is content and vendor work, not platform engineering. Starting it now costs nothing from the build queue and it has the longest external lead time of anything here.

D3

Can we get a real Prodma data export?

What we have is application source plus a menu and permission export. There is no CARI, STOK or FATURA data anywhere in it, so the demo org is seeded with synthetic Turkish manufacturer data. A SQL Server export of even three tables would change that.

Why it matters: it decides whether the demo is credible to a domain expert, and it is the only way to validate the entity model against real cardinality and real edge cases rather than against a generator.

D4

Which of the original 24 entity types do we actually want?

The first proposal had 24 types. The org shipped with 14. Three obvious omissions have just been added — fixed-asset, cost-center and offset, each a whole Prodma module with its own forms — taking it to 17.

Why it matters: the remaining seven were dropped without a recorded rationale, so we cannot tell deliberate compression from oversight. Worth reconstructing the original list before modelling anything else on top.

D5

Is pre-printed form output a requirement?

Deterministic PDF and archive output, and whether documents must align to pre-printed stationery, materially change the printing work in Gap 11.

Why it matters: low effort to answer, and it is the difference between a reporting feature and a pixel-exact layout engine. Cheap to ask, expensive to guess wrong.

OPEN

How does a posting reliably cause its journal entry?

The only remaining open question, and the sharpest one. An enforcing write can refuse a transition; making one cause a second write in the same commit is different. Post-commit reactions give "late, or never", which for statutory books is not a retry problem but an accounting one.

Requirement given: make it reliable. That rules out best-effort reactions for the statutory path, and points at either an in-transaction hook for side effects or a real outbox with idempotency keys and compensation states. Decide before Step 5.

D1 ✓

Document lines: hybrid, and already running

Lines stay a JSONB array carrying product_id, and the reference is also materialised as a graph edge. Atomic one-row writes plus a traversable graph. Inventory is now real: 60 stock movements sit behind the product balances.

Commits us to: the two layers can drift — nothing yet enforces that a line's product_id matches its edge. That reconciliation is a funnel responsibility, and it is the price of the hybrid.

D2 ✓

Model properly, mock the integrations

Build the statutory model — books, chart of accounts, document types — as if real, with GİB/e-Fatura integration mocked behind the same interface.

Commits us to: the interface has to be right even though nothing crosses it yet, since swapping a mock for a real integrator later is only cheap if the seam was honest from the start.

There is no Prodma business data to import. The org now holds 238 entities across 10 populated types and 473 edges, all synthetic and deterministic.

Support every module Prodma supports, without mirroring 422 tables. Three modules with no covering type have been added: fixed-asset, cost-center, offset. Now 17 types.

Document output via reaction scripts

Correct call, and the one place reactions are unambiguously the right tool — rendering is post-hoc by nature and needs nothing from the write transaction.

**But it has one precondition, and a spike showed it isn't met yet.** I took a *posted* invoice in the live org and changed its total with a plain SDK write:

No refusal, no approval, no audit trail. Restored and verified.

Confirmed: hooks are `beforeCreate` / `afterCreate` / `beforeDelete` only. **No update hook exists**, and none of them receive a transaction — the context carries only org, user, env.

## Spike 3 result: an imperative guard is advisory

```
FTR2028000020
  guard read status:        draft      → guard_decision: allow
  status when write lands:  posted
  approved_write_landed:    true
  guard_was_advisory:       true       (restored, verified)
```

The guard read "draft" and approved. The document became "posted" before the write landed. The approved write went through anyway — onto a posted document.

So a script's check and its write are **two separate transactions**, which they must be: `client.query` is forced `READ ONLY`, so the write cannot share it. That's a real TOCTOU window, not a theoretical one.

This sharpens the earlier answer. Within "Behavior-as-writer" there are two very different mechanisms:

- **Imperative** `client.entities.update` in a script → check is advisory, race window open
- **Declared outputs** → commit atomically with the window, savepoints, genuine atomicity

Your architecture works — but only through declared outputs, not through if-statements in reaction scripts.

## The best architecture for #1

The question is how posting an invoice reliably causes its journal entry. Three candidates:

| | Atomic? | Works when a *human* posts? |
|---|---|---|
| Declared outputs | Yes | **No** — only when a Behavior is the initiator |
| In-transaction hook | Yes | Yes — sits at the write path |
| Outbox + saga | No, eventually consistent | Yes |

Declared outputs are elegant and already exist, but they only cover agent-initiated posting. A human clicking "post" in the UI isn't a Behavior run, and the journal entry must appear either way. That rules it out as the whole answer.

**My recommendation is a two-tier split, drawn on whether the effect is inside the database or outside it:**

**Internal consequences — journal entry, stock movement — go in the transaction.** These are same-database writes. There is no reason to make them eventually consistent, and an outbox here buys nothing while opening a window where the books are provably wrong. The seam already exists: `runMutationGate` runs inside `sql.begin`, holds the row lock, and receives both current and proposed values. What's missing is narrow — an update hook that can *emit* rather than only *deny*.

**External consequences — GİB e-fatura submission, email, PDF archival — go in an outbox.** These genuinely cannot be transactional; you can't roll back an HTTP POST. They need idempotency keys, retry classification, and compensation states. That's register gap 10, and it's real work, but it's confined to the boundary where it's unavoidable.

The reason I'd argue this isn't the overengineering you were worried about: it's **one hook at one seam that already has the transaction**. Not a framework. The current hook registry has no update hook at all, so this is additive and small — and it's the same seam that enforces the invariant, so enforcement and consequence share one place rather than two.

## Why #4 matters

`Ortak` means "common/shared" — 12 forms. If it holds shared reference data like units of measure, currencies, or tax rates, those are values every document already references as bare strings (`unit: "ADET"`, `vat_rate: 20`). Today nothing validates them and nothing can report across them. That's the kind of omission that looks cosmetic and then blocks a tax report.

And with ~7 of the original 24 unrecovered, we can't tell deliberate compression from oversight. `Stok Hizmet` (service items) is visible in the menu, for instance — if that was dropped, a service invoice has no product to point at.

**Best way to resolve it: stop doing archaeology.** Don't hunt the old artifact. Re-derive the list from ground truth — the EDMX/CSDL model in the source has 503 DbSets, and the `M_MENU` export has 533 rows of real screens. The original 24 was itself derived from those, so going back to the source is both more authoritative and cheaper than finding a document that recorded someone's earlier reading of it.

Section 03

How every other ERP solves this

The write chokepoint is not a Lobu-specific design taste. It is the load-bearing invariant of the entire ERP category, and every serious system in the space has the same two mechanisms under different names.

OdooNetSuiteSalesforceLobu today
Write chokepoint ORM write() record submit DML absent ~22 bypasses
Hook inside the transaction @api.constrains, write() override beforeSubmit before update trigger none no update hook at all
Posted document immutable yes yes n/a no proven mutable
Schema extensible at runtime partial custom records custom objects ahead no deploy needed
Reasoning layer producing documents no no bolt-on ahead declared outputs, atomic

The counterintuitive part. A traditional ERP gets a lot of enforcement for free from the screen: Prodma's permission model is 5 roles × 101 screens, and the form decides what can be typed at all. An agent has no screen. It holds the whole API surface and none of the implicit constraint the form was providing.

So an agentic ERP needs more enforcement at the persistence layer than a conventional one, not less — the screen was doing invisible work and it is now gone. That is the direct answer to whether the hook is overengineering: in this architecture it is more load-bearing than in the systems that already ship one.

Where the agentic version genuinely wins, and it is not the data entry:

  • Exceptions. Most ERP labour is short shipments, price mismatches, duplicate invoices. Conventional systems answer these with more screens; reasoning over context is a better fit, and it is the strongest argument for the whole approach.
  • Intent instead of transaction entry. "Restock what we are short of before the Konya shipment" makes the document an output of reasoning rather than an input to a form.
  • Rules that explain themselves. Odoo raises "you cannot modify a posted entry". An agent can cite the period, and propose the legal reversal instead.
  • Configuration without a consultant — runtime schema change is already real here.

And where it is worse, which is why the split matters: a model in the write path is a category error, audit gets harder because reasoning traces must be kept alongside the deterministic rule, and an agent per document does not scale to ten thousand invoices a day. Deterministic path for the 95%, agent for the exceptions.

Artifact updated: https://claude.ai/code/artifact/899626f9-7f89-4c8d-b52a-f00a0201e962

## Spike 3: declared outputs *can* carry it

`promoteBehaviorEntityOutput` takes a `tx`, and the code is emphatic:

> *"Duplicate exact keys and unexpected persistence errors **fail the completion transaction**: declared outputs are an atomic contract, not a best-effort side channel that may silently lose rows."* — and on error, *"rolling back window completion."*

Outputs are "named top-level arrays the Behavior persists after each completed window" — **plural**. So a Behavior can declare `invoices` and `journalEntries` and both land in one commit, or neither does.

**That means Spike 5 is already solved for the agent-initiated path.** What it doesn't cover is a human clicking "post" in the UI — that isn't a Behavior run, and the journal entry has to appear either way. So the gap is narrower than I framed it: not "we need a side-effect mechanism," but "the human path needs the one the agent path already has."

## Task 2: re-derived from the EDMX

`PrdomaModel.csdl` — **422 EntityTypes, 96 prefixes**. Our 17 types cover `CARI` 52, `STOK` 32, `MUHASEBE` 30, `FATURA` 11, `FIYAT` 10, `SIPARIS` 9, `TEKLIF` 7, `CEK` 7, `AMBAR` 7, `RECETE` 6, `SABIT` 4, `MAHSUP` 3.

`Ortak` resolves: `LK_*` (13) are lookup/enum tables — `LK_AY_ISIMLERI` is literally month names. Mostly enum values, not entity types. The exceptions worth promoting are **`DOVIZ`/`DOVIZ_KUR`** (currency + FX rate) and `ULKE`, because documents reference them as bare strings today and nothing validates them.

Genuinely missing business domains, ranked: **`SERVIS` 11** (after-sales), **`KARGO` 10** (shipping), `KREDI` 7, **`E_*` 5** (`E_FATURA`/`E_ARSIV` — this *is* the GİB surface), **`KALIP` 5** (molds — manufacturing-specific), `IHRACAT`/`ITHALAT` 4 each, **`KESIN_MALIYET` 4** (actual costing), `PLAN` 4, **`PARTI` 3** (lot/batch traceability).

Two stand out for a manufacturer: **`PARTI`** and **`KESIN_MALIYET`**. And **`URETIM` is 20 tables against a single `work-order` type** — the largest under-modelling by far.

## Modern ERP, and what "agentic" actually changes

Every serious ERP has the same two mechanisms under different names:

| | Odoo | NetSuite | Salesforce | Lobu today |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Write chokepoint | ORM `write()` | record submit | DML | **absent** — ~22 bypasses |
| In-transaction hook | `@api.constrains` | `beforeSubmit` | `before update` | **no update hook at all** |
| Posted doc immutable | yes | yes | n/a | **no** — proven |
| Runtime schema change | partial | custom records | custom objects | **ahead** |
| Reasoning layer → documents | no | no | bolt-on | **ahead** |

Odoo cannot write `account_move` except through the ORM. That's not a stylistic choice — it's what lets it promise a posted entry can't change. Lobu is genuinely ahead on two axes and missing the one that defines the category.

**The counterintuitive part, and it's the real answer to your overengineering worry.** A traditional ERP gets enormous enforcement for free from the screen. Prodma's own model proves it: 5 roles × 101 *screens*, and the form decides what can be typed at all. An agent has no screen. It holds the entire API surface with none of the implicit constraint the form was providing.

So an agentic ERP needs **more** enforcement at the persistence layer than a conventional one, not less. The screen was doing invisible work and it's gone. The hook isn't overengineering here — it's *more* load-bearing than in the systems that already ship one.

**Where agentic genuinely wins** — and it isn't data entry, which is the thing everyone demos. It's **exceptions**. Most ERP labour is short shipments, price mismatches, duplicate invoices, and conventional systems answer those with more screens. Reasoning over context is a much better fit. Second is intent over entry: "restock what we're short of before the Konya shipment" makes the document an output of reasoning rather than an input to a form. Third, rules that explain themselves — Odoo says "you cannot modify a posted entry"; an agent can cite the period and offer the legal reversal.

Where it's worse, which is why the split is essential rather than a compromise: a model in the write path is a category error; audit gets *harder* because you must retain the reasoning trace alongside the deterministic rule; and an agent per document doesn't scale to ten thousand invoices a day. Deterministic for the 95%, agent for the exceptions.

**So the architecture is three layers, and the ordering is the whole point:**

1. **Ledger** — deterministic, non-bypassable. Odoo's ORM equivalent. No model, ever. Freeze, period, numbering, referential integrity.
2. **Operations** — agentic, via declared outputs, committing atomically *through* layer 1. Verified working today.
3. **Interaction** — chat plus generic CRUD pages. Already your stated position.

Your instinct got layer 2 exactly right. The spikes showed layer 1 doesn't exist yet — a posted invoice is mutable, and an imperative guard is advisory.

Confidence:
- **Declared outputs are atomic across multiple outputs — 90.** Read from source including explicit rollback semantics; I did not execute a two-output Behavior end to end.
- **EDMX cluster map — 95.** Parsed directly from the 422-type model.
- **ERP comparison — 85.** Odoo/Salesforce mechanics I'm confident on; NetSuite `beforeSubmit` is from knowledge, not verified today.

Next actions:
1. Decide whether the human "post" path gets the in-transaction hook, or whether human posting routes through a Behavior so declared outputs cover both.
2. Add `PARTI` (lot/batch) and `KESIN_MALIYET` (actual costing) — the two most defensible additions for a manufacturer.
3. `URETIM` at 20 tables against one type needs a modelling pass of its own.
4. Run a real two-output Behavior to confirm the atomicity claim executes as documented.

Summary:
## 1. Primary Request and Intent

**Overarching (inherited):** A gap analysis — explicitly **NOT a migration** — of whether **Prodma**, a Turkish manufacturing ERP (.NET 4.6.1, WinForms/DevExpress, SQL Server, EF EDMX, 422 tables / 453 screens, source at `/Users/burakemre/Downloads/emre_project`), could be rebuilt on **Lobu**. Purpose: "to see where lobu lacks." Audience is Prodma's owner, a domain expert.

**Intents this session, in order:**
1. Resume: verify whether agent #11's held work already shipped, "but we need to make sure we fill the gaps."
2. Kill the stale local `lobu run`; confirm prod is healthy.
3. Delete dead feeds; confirm ERP prod is up to date; explain where `acme-usage` came from.
4. Fix why prod ERP data was never populated; seed it properly.
5. Confirm whether seed data came from real Prodma data; get exact entity-type counts.
6. Locate the Excel exports in `~/Downloads`; determine whether entity types are missing vs the original plan.
7. Read the YETKI permission sheets, recover the original 24-type list, and make prod carry "all the relevant stuff."
8. Answer D1–D5; challenge whether the hook system is overengineering, proposing enforcement in reaction scripts.
9. Make Spike 5 reliable; talk to (or kill) the funnel agent; run spikes; update the artifact; explain why Behaviors-as-mutators can't already enforce.
10. Re-derive entity types from the EDMX; spike declared outputs; compare against modern ERP technology as "an agentic version of it."

## 2. Key Technical Concepts

- **Behavior-as-writer vs Behavior-as-reaction** — the central architectural distinction. A Behavior that *performs* a write can enforce (atomic, in-transaction). A *reaction* cannot (post-commit, read-only sandbox).
- **`runMutationGate` runs inside `sql.begin`** with `sql: tx`, holding the row's `FOR UPDATE` lock (`entity-management.ts:696`). This is a true chokepoint.
- **Reactions are post-commit** — `manage_entity.ts` comment at the `queue()` call: *"Post-commit: ... queue() runs AFTER the entity tx + change event so the approval (run + event + notification) is never rolled back with the edit."*
- **Sandbox forces `SET TRANSACTION READ ONLY`** at `sandbox/client-sdk.ts:263`.
- **Declared outputs are atomic** — `promoteBehaviorEntityOutput` takes a `tx`; *"Duplicate exact keys and unexpected persistence errors fail the completion transaction: declared outputs are an atomic contract, not a best-effort side channel that may silently lose rows"* (`promote-keyed-entities.ts:438`); on error *"rolling back window completion"* (`:667`); savepoints at `:214`. `outputs?: Record<string, BehaviorOutput>` — plural named arrays.
- **`entity-hooks.ts` has only `beforeCreate` / `afterCreate` / `beforeDelete`** — **no update hook**, and `EntityHookContext` carries only `organizationId`, `userId`, `env` — no tx.
- **Three write-path gaps proven in prod:** (a) a declared `default` does NOT satisfy a `required` field on create; (b) `entities.update` validates the PATCH not the merged result; (c) a soft-deleted entity still holds its name.
- **`lobu link`** binds a directory to (context, org) in `.lobu/project.json` and **arms `apply`'s project-link guard** (`--force` = "Bypass the project-link guard if context/org don't match").
- **`lobu memory exec` takes inline source, not a file path.**
- **`entity_types` is NOT in the SDK sandbox queryable allowlist** (allowed: behavior_versions, behaviors, canvas_windows, channel_messages, connections, connector_definitions, entities, entity_relationship_types, entity_relationships, event_classifications, events, feeds, oauth_clients, oauth_tokens, user).
- **`consecutive_failures` is on `feeds`**, not `connections`.
- **Prod DB pod renamed** to `lobu-db-prod-1`; namespace `summaries-prod`; DB name `owletto`; `organization` uses camelCase `createdAt`.
- **ERP category invariant:** every serious ERP has a non-bypassable transaction-bound write chokepoint plus an in-transaction hook — Odoo ORM `write()` + `@api.constrains`; NetSuite record submit + `beforeSubmit`; Salesforce DML + `before update` trigger.

## 3. Files and Code Sections

Version-owned fields (name, description, prompt, sources) are immutable here — use createVersion. Status is not patchable here (a Behavior is retired via delete → archived).
---
operations.execute — Execute a connector action. OBJECT signature: execute({ connection_id: number, operation_key: string, input?: object, idempotency_key?: string, behavior_source?: { behavior_id: number, window_id: number } }). connector_key is not accepted. A durable idempotency_key replays the original run instead of repeating the external request.

behaviors.completeWindow — Submit LLM-extracted data for a Behavior window. Requires a signed window_token.
---
behaviors.create — Create a Behavior. Requires slug and agent_id; window/manual Behaviors also need prompt or skills. Declare named outputs as `{ entity, key, name? }` or `{ event }`, or omit outputs for a Canvas/reaction-only Behavior. Event output rows are standard drafts with required content and optional title, metadata, author, source_url, occurred_at, parent_event_id, payload_type, and idempotency_key. Outputs require window execution. Each sources[] entry requires `name` and a read-only SELECT/WITH `query` projecting an `id` column; optional `context: true` marks the source as context-o

behaviors.createFromVersion — Create Behaviors for multiple entities from an existing Behavior version.
