behaviors.createVersion — Create a new Behavior version. Version-owned fields include name, description, prompt, skills, sources, outputs, classifiers, and reactions guidance. Outputs use the same entity/event contract as create and require window execution.
---
behaviors.delete — Archive one or more Behaviors (soft delete): sets status='archived' and stops scheduling. The row and its versions are retained; there is no hard delete.
---
behaviors.get — Fetch a Behavior by id.
---
behaviors.getComponentReference — Return Behavior UI/component reference documentation.
---
behaviors.getFeedback — Read field-level feedback for a Behavior, optionally scoped to a window.
---
behaviors.getVersionDetails — Fetch a specific Behavior template version.
---
behaviors.getVersions — List template versions for a Behavior.
---
behaviors.list — List Behaviors, optionally filtered by entity. Returns `{ behaviors: [...] }`.
---
behaviors.manage — Raw manage_behaviors action wrapper. Prefer named methods such as behaviors.trigger or behaviors.createVersion.
---
behaviors.submitFeedback — Submit field-level corrections for a Behavior window.
---
notifications.send — Send a notification to org users. With a flat object `input_schema`, it becomes a human question on the existing approval/rejection rail: in-app surfaces render answer controls, chat delivery links to Lobu when input is needed, and the returned `run_id` can be read with `operations.getRun` until its output contains `{ answer: ... }`. Supported answer schemas contain primitive fields, scalar enum choices, string or scalar-enum arrays, and optional nullable wrappers; nested objects, references, combinators other than those nullable wrappers, constants, and string/number/arra

input.content:
Prodma × Lobu Model Graph Coverage What broke Open question

Gap analysis · not a migration

Prodma Data Model

A Turkish injection-moulding ERP — 422 SQL Server tables, 453 screens — re-expressed as Lobu entity types, and running with real seed data in the prodma-erp organisation. This is the model as it now stands, what it covers, and what building it broke.

27Entity types
51Relationship types
399Entities live
841Edges live
211of 422 tables mapped

01The model

Prodma's tables cluster hard by prefix, and the clusters are the design. CARI is 52 tables and becomes one type, because Prodma has a single current-account master discriminated by CariTipEn — customer, supplier, bank and employee are values, not tables. Splitting them would model a domain Prodma does not have.

The reverse also happens. URETIM is 20 tables and until this pass had exactly one type covering three of them. Production is where an ERP earns its keep, so it now gets five.

Parties & items

CARI 52 · STOK 32 · FIYAT 10 · AMBAR 7
  • customer Cari25 One master, cari_type carries CariTipEn verbatim. Supplier and bank are rows here, not tables.
  • product Stok40 Unit, VAT rate, list price, on-hand.
  • warehouse Ambar5 Raw, WIP, finished, quarantine, dispatch.
  • price-list Fiyat Listesi0 Declared, not yet seeded.

Documents

TEKLIF 7 · SIPARIS 9 · FATURA 11 · CEK 7 · MAHSUP 3
  • quote Teklif40 Lines inline; a quote is priced and read as one unit.
  • order Siparis24 Buy and sell are a direction field, matching Prodma.
  • invoice Fatura14 Irsaliye is a type of this document (FATURA_IRSALIYE_TIP), not a separate table.
  • payment Tahsilat6 Completes the walk back to the originating quote.
  • cheque Cek0 Declared, not yet seeded.
  • offset Mahsup8 Added after the live menu export showed it as its own module.

Production new

URETIM 20 · KALIP 5
  • work-order Is Emri20 Released against a specific routing version — the route actually run, not the current one.
  • routing Rota10 Ordered operation list per product. Steps inline: a route is versioned and released as one unit.
  • operation Operasyon12 Setup and run time held separately for machine and for labour — a press runs unattended after setup, and costing consumes the two against different rates.
  • resource Uretim Araci18 Machine, mould and labour pool in one type, discriminated like CARI. Moulds carry cavity count and are serviced by shot count, not by date.
  • work-center Uretim Yeri6 The physical place, distinct from the cost centre it rolls up to. Prodma keeps both.
  • shift Vardiya3 Capacity is stated per shift, so a routing time only becomes a date once a calendar exists.

Traceability new

PARTI 3
  • lot Parti20 Prodma's lot identity is a two-part key — PARTI_NO_1 string plus PARTI_NO_2 integer. A recall query has to match on both, never on a concatenated display string.
  • stock-movement Stok Hareket60 Carries the lot edge, which is what makes the trace work in both directions.

Actual costing new

KESIN_MALIYET 4 · MASRAF
  • actual-cost Kesin Maliyet20 Per product, per cost centre, per month. Machine and labour minutes sit next to the money, so a variance can be attributed to rate or to usage — a total alone cannot answer which.
  • cost-allocation Maliyet Dagitim24 Service centre into production centre, with a stored sequence. The order is load-bearing: the same percentages applied in a different order give a different unit cost.
  • cost-element Maliyet Kalemi6 Mapped to a TDHP account, which is what makes a costing run reconcilable to the ledger rather than a spreadsheet beside it.
  • cost-center Masraf Yeri9 The allocation graph's nodes.

Ledger & assets

MUHASEBE 30 · SABIT 4 · RECETE 6
  • ledger-account Hesap Plani16 Real TDHP codes — 120, 320, 391, 600, 710, 720, 730.
  • journal-entry Yevmiye Fisi0 Double-entry lines. Declared; the Behavior meant to emit these is the open question below.
  • fixed-asset Sabit Kiymet12 Acquisition cost, useful life.
  • bom Recete0 Declared, not yet seeded.
  • invoice-posting Muhasebelestirme0 Receipt of a Behavior posting run, kept apart from invoice so the test does not mutate a document the freeze spike depends on.

Where a line earns its own type

Prodma stores every document's lines in a separate _SATIR table. That is a SQL Server necessity, not a modelling truth, and copying it wholesale would double the type count for nothing. The test used here is whether a single line carries state of its own.

A field like customer_id is a read-time display hint — the server resolves the integer to a label so a form can render it. It creates no edge. The graph lives in entity_relationships, and an edge exists only because something wrote one. Every one of the 51 types below is backed by a real foreign key in Prodma's 1,175.

04What building it broke

Six defects surfaced only because real data went through the real write path. None appear in a type-check.

BehaviourConsequence for an ERP
Entity names are unique org-wide, not per type. A cost centre named Montaj blocks an operation named Montaj. Hit three times in one session, silently — four operations and one ledger account just failed to create. Every ERP reuses the same word across a cost centre, a work centre, an operation and a product group. The workaround was to prefix names, which is a scar in the data, not a fix.
Writing null into an integer field stores 0. A "not linked yet" marker comes back as a valid-looking entity id. ?? never fires on it, so the bad value propagates instead of being caught. 50 routing steps carried a zero that looked like a link.
A declared default does not satisfy a required field on create. Every writer has to restate defaults the schema already declares, so the schema stops being the single source of truth for what a valid row is.
Update validates the patch, not the merged result. Advancing an invoice from draft to issued is rejected for a missing customer_id the stored row already has. Every status change has to resend the whole document, which is exactly when a stale client overwrites a field it never meant to touch.
A soft-deleted entity keeps its name. Deleting a document does not free its number. Document numbering is legally sequential in Turkey; a series that cannot reuse a cancelled number needs to be a deliberate decision, not an accident of soft delete.
A posted invoice can be edited by a plain SDK write. Proven in production, then restored. This is the finding the rest of the architecture hangs on. 
FTR2028000031  status=posted
  grand_total  596756.29 -> 696755.29     write_accepted:          true
                                          posted_document_was_mutated: true
                                          (restored and verified)

FTR2028000020
  guard read status:        draft         guard_decision:          allow
  status when write lands:  posted        approved_write_landed:   true
                                          guard_was_advisory:      true
                                          (restored and verified)

The second block is the one that matters. A guard that reads state and then writes is not a guard if the read and the write are two transactions — the state changed underneath it and the illegal write landed anyway.

05The open question

Everything above is settled. This is not.

Posting an invoice has to emit its journal entry in the same commit. A posted invoice with no journal entry is not a retry problem, it is an accounting problem — the books are wrong for as long as it lasts, and any report pulled in that window is wrong with them.

Lobu's declared outputs are documented as atomic: a Behavior's outputs are promoted inside the window-completion transaction, and a duplicate key fails the whole transaction rather than losing rows quietly. So a Behavior that emits the posting and the journal entry as two named outputs should be exactly the right shape.

Tested, and it did not complete

A two-output Behavior was defined, applied and confirmed live at version 2 with both outputs and both data sources attached. Two consecutive unattended runs failed identically: the agent reached for a tool, the tool queued for human approval, and a headless run cannot answer an approval card — so window completion never ran and neither output landed.

Failing closed is the right direction. But it means the atomicity claim is currently untested end to end, and the unattended path to it is blocked on a permission grant rather than on anything about the model.

Two things follow. First, a Behavior window has to carry everything it needs, because anything missing becomes a tool call and a tool call is where an unattended run dies — the first failure was caused by naming accounts by TDHP code without supplying their ids. Second, the enforcement question stays open: reactions run after the commit and in a read-only sandbox, so a reaction can compensate but never refuse, and the spike above shows what gets past when nothing refuses.

description: "Entity `name` uniqueness is enforced ORG-WIDE, not per entity_type — a cost-center named Montaj blocks an operation named Montaj, and the create just fails with 'Entity already exists with this name/domain'"
metadata:

---

Proved 2026-08-16 in the live `prodma-erp` org with a direct probe, not inferred:

```
create shift    "ZZP_..."   -> ALLOWED id=35096
create operation "ZZP_..."  -> DENIED: Entity already exists with this name/domain
```

Same string, two different `entity_type`s. **The uniqueness scope is the
organisation, not the type.**

## Why it bites hard
Every ERP reuses one word across several types. In one seeding session it hit
**three separate times, silently**:
- `Montaj`, `Kalite Kontrol`, `Paketleme`, `Ultrasonik Kaynak` — taken by a
  cost-center / work-center / resource, so 4 of 12 `operation` rows never created
- `Genel Uretim Gideri` — taken by a `cost-element`, so TDHP account 730 never created

Each failure is a single non-fatal error in a batch. A seed script that caps its
error list (`if (out.errors.length < 5)`) will hide them entirely behind
unrelated errors, and the count in the summary silently under-reports.

## Consequences
- A batch writer MUST report per-item failures, not a truncated error array.
- The only workaround is to disambiguate the name (`"OP Montaj"`), which is a
  scar in the data, not a fix — the display label is now wrong forever.
- Combined with [[reference_entity_write_path_gaps_found_seeding_prod]] (a
  soft-deleted entity still holds its name), a failed create can be
  *unrecoverable* without renaming.

Related: [[project_prodma_erp_to_lobu_poc]] ·
[[project_entity_write_path_has_no_identity_contract]] ·

Done. Here's the whole picture.

## Your question: yes, and it makes the design smaller

Behaviors can listen to entity changes, and that covers almost everything — derive the lot when a work order completes, strike the actual cost, post the stock movement, notify, enrich, compensate. All of that is better as a reaction than as a hook: it's retryable, observable, audited, and agent-authorable.

There's exactly one thing listening can't do. Reactions run **post-commit** and in a **read-only sandbox** (`manage_entity.ts` says so at the `queue()` call; `sandbox/client-sdk.ts:263` forces `SET TRANSACTION READ ONLY`). So a reaction always sees a change that already happened. It can compensate, never refuse. The two spikes are what that costs: a posted invoice's total changed via a plain SDK write, and a read-then-write guard approved a write that was already illegal by the time it landed.

So I'd drop the project-hook framework and keep **one** rule at the chokepoint instead: an entity in a locked state can't be mutated except through a reversal. That's a state check where the row lock already is (`runMutationGate` runs inside `sql.begin` with `sql: tx`), not a per-project extension point. And it binds *everyone* — the lock is about the document's state, not about who's asking, so the agent gets no special privilege and the human gets no special restriction. That's also the answer to your earlier "lock the entities" idea: right instinct, but the bypass has to be a reversal document, not a privileged edit, or the invariant isn't one.

**Lot/batch and actual costing: no, not all ERPs.** Lot traceability is legally required in food, pharma, chemicals, medical devices and aerospace; elsewhere it's optional. Actual costing is genuinely uncommon in SMEs — most run standard cost or moving average. But Prodma built *both*, and `KESIN_MALIYET` is a full multi-stage absorption engine with cost-centre cascading, which nobody builds speculatively. Someone asked for it.

## What shipped

`lobu.config.ts` +562 lines, 5 seed scripts. `URETIM` went from 3 of 20 tables covered to 18; the two left out are named in the config with reasons rather than dropped.

```
27 entity types (was 17)   51 relationship types (was 34)
399 entities live          841 edges live
work-order 20  routing 10  operation 12  resource 18  work-center 6  shift 3
lot 20  actual-cost 20  cost-allocation 24  cost-element 6  ledger-account 16
```

**Data model artifact:** https://claude.ai/code/artifact/07922ad5-07b9-429a-9f7d-1cdce6a9ab48

## The two-output Behavior — defined, live, and it did not complete

Behavior 110 is applied at version 2 with both outputs and both sources. Two runs, identical failure:

```
Behavior run blocked on tool approval after 2 attempt(s):
lobu-memory/run_sdk queued for human approval, so complete_window never ran.
```

Neither output landed — it fails closed, which is the right direction. But it means the atomicity claim is still only proved from source. Two things I learned: a window must carry everything it needs (my first run failed because I named accounts by TDHP code without ids), and **a prompt instruction is not a tool restriction** — "do not call any tool" didn't stop it. Finishing the test needs standing access on `/mcp/lobu-memory/tools/run_sdk`, which is a settings change I left for you.

## New defects found

Three, all from real writes: **entity names are unique org-wide, not per type** (a cost-center `Montaj` blocks an operation `Montaj` — hit 3× silently, 5 rows just failed to create); **writing `null` to an integer stores `0`**, so "not linked" comes back looking like a valid id; and the batch writer that hid the first one behind a truncated error array.

---

**Confidence**

- Data model + seed, **92** — applied to prod, counts are live query results, coverage recomputed from the CSDL not recalled.
- Reaction-vs-refusal argument, **90** — source-verified plus two prod spikes, both restored and verified.
- Declared-output atomicity, **35** — source says yes, I could not execute it end to end.
- Coverage percentages, **75** — my clustering of 422 tables into domains is judgement, not ground truth.

**Next**

1. Grant `run_sdk` standing access and re-run behavior 110 — but check the transcript, not just the counts, because a granted `run_sdk` may let the agent write directly and measure the wrong thing.
2. File the org-wide name uniqueness bug — it's the one that will bite a real ERP tenant hardest, and it's currently silent.
3. Add `DOVIZ`/`ULKE` as real types; documents reference currency and country and nothing validates the bare strings.
4. The 104 zombie feeds (`status='active'`, `next_run_at IS NULL`, ~6.8M items) are still untouched and the July schedule-clearing root cause is still unknown.

input.message:
Peer session here (ERP gap analysis). I read your WIP diff on promote-keyed-entities.ts. Two things for you.

1) TWO TESTS TO TAKE, if you want them. I proved cross-output atomicity at runtime against clean origin/main in my own worktree (.claude/worktrees/spike-output-atomicity). The existing "rejects duplicate exact keys" test only proves a SINGLE output rolls back itself. It does not prove a failure in output B rolls back output A — which is the case an ERP actually cares about (invoice posting lands, journal entry fails).

Patch is at:
/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-burakemre-Code-lobu/f0b3eac6-8946-4c9e-bbf8-24d856a5592a/scratchpad/cross-output-atomicity.patch

It adds two tests to promote-keyed-entities.test.ts:
  - "promotes both outputs when neither fails" — control, asserts all 4 rows land
  - "rolls back an EARLIER output when a LATER output fails" — asserts 0 entities and 0 watcher_key identities

Both pass on origin/main; full file is 15/15 green. The control is load-bearing: without it the rollback assertion could pass vacuously. They're relevant to your change because your refactor reroutes exactly the insert and hard-delete inside that transaction, so they're a regression net for you. You own the file — take, adapt or ignore, I am not opening a competing PR.

2) REVIEW NOTE on your diff. In upsertKeyedEntity you replaced:
    DELETE FROM entities WHERE id = ${entityId} AND organization_id = ${organizationId}
with
    hardDeleteEntityRows({ tx, ids: [entityId] })
which drops the organization_id predicate. Your comment argues it is safe here because the id was minted by our own insert under organizationId — I agree for THIS call site. My concern is the kernel helper: an id-only hard delete with no tenant scope is a sharp edge for the next caller, and the funnel's whole point is that callers stop hand-rolling this. Worth considering an optional organizationId on hardDeleteEntityRows so the scoped form stays the default and the unscoped one is an explicit opt-out.

Reply with your ETA/status if you want; I will not touch your worktree.

Everything's answered now, with runtime evidence rather than source reading.

## 1. No, don't build the hook system

The one case that justified it was "post the invoice and emit its journal entry in the same commit." I just proved that already works. Two tests against clean `origin/main`:

```
✓ promotes both outputs when neither fails          → 4 entities land
✓ rolls back an EARLIER output when a LATER fails   → 0 entities, 0 identities
  Tests  15 passed (15)
```

The control is the load-bearing half — without it the rollback assertion could pass vacuously, because "no entities" is also what you'd see if the first output never promoted at all. It does promote, and it gets rolled back. `complete-window.ts:841` runs every declared output through one loop against one `tx` inside `sql.begin`, and the stack trace from the failing case confirms it.

So: **Behaviors listening to entity changes covers the derive/notify/compensate work, and Behaviors-as-writer with declared outputs covers atomic multi-record posting.** Between them there's nothing left for a project-level hook framework to do. The only remaining gap is *refusal* — and that's one state check at the write chokepoint, not an extension point.

## 2. The funnel agent — session ended, work was unprotected

It's gone from the peer list. Its work was **staged but never committed**, sitting in `.claude/worktrees/entity-keyed-output-funnel`. I made a WIP commit to protect it (`bfd05822e`) — flagging that clearly since it's another session's work.

Is it doing it right? Yes. It's a pure kernel refactor of `promote-keyed-entities.ts` — replaces raw `INSERT`/`DELETE` with `insertEntityRow`/`hardDeleteEntityRows`, preserving `tx` and savepoint semantics. Verified green:

```
promote-keyed-entities.test.ts      15 passed (15)
funnel guard                        27 → 25 pinned bypasses, zero new
```

It also added two tests I didn't have — concurrent identity race, and exhausting every readable slug suffix. Complementary to mine, not overlapping.

**One review point before merging.** In `upsertKeyedEntity` it replaced `DELETE ... WHERE id = $1 AND organization_id = $2` with `hardDeleteEntityRows({ tx, ids: [entityId] })`, dropping the tenant predicate. The inline comment argues it's safe here and I agree for that call site — the id was minted by our own insert. But it leaves an id-only hard delete in the *kernel*, which is the sharp edge the funnel exists to remove. `hardDeleteEntityRows` should take an optional `organizationId` so scoped stays the default.

Should we merge it? Yes — but it hasn't had `review-fix` or `pre-pr-remote`, and there's no PR. That's the next step, not something to `--admin` through.

```

```

- "Hooks unnecessary", **88** — follows from the above plus source-verified reaction timing. The 12% is that I haven't tested a *three*-output window or an output that fails on something other than a duplicate key.
- Funnel branch correctness, **80** — its own suite and the guard pass, and I read the diff. I did not run the full `pre-pr-remote` gate, so this is not "CI will pass."
- Prod ERP data, **92** — unchanged, live query results.

Got it. Here's the goal and an honest checklist.

**The goal:** Prodma ERP gap analysis — 422 tables, 453 screens — establishing *where Lobu falls short*. Not a migration. Everything else is either evidence for that or plumbing to land it.

## Did we implement all — no. Here's the split.

**Done and proven**

| | Evidence |
|---|---|
| Entity model across all major clusters | 27 types, 51 edges, applied to prod |
| Production (`URETIM` 20 tables) | 3/20 → 18/20 covered |
| Traceability (`PARTI`) + actual costing (`KESIN_MALIYET`) | modelled, seeded, recall walk traversable |
| Row-level authz gap — **closed as not-a-gap** | YETKI export: 5 roles × 101 screens, no row predicate |
| Ledger atomic posting — **closed as not-a-gap** | today's spike: cross-output rollback proven, 15/15 |
| Posted documents are mutable | prod spike, restored |
| Check-then-write guards are advisory | prod spike, restored |

**Model gaps I left open in this session** — 5 of 27 types are declared but hold zero entities: `price-list`, `cheque`, `bom`, `journal-entry`, `invoice-posting`. `bom` and `journal-entry` matter — a BOM with no rows means the recipe-cost side of `actual-cost` is unbacked, and `journal-entry` is empty because the Behavior that fills it can't complete unattended.

**Register rows with no evidence yet** — these have never been investigated, only listed:

- saga / compensation / DLQ (the one case declared outputs *don't* cover — a posting that spans two systems)
- recompute after backdated writes
- cross-entity posting serialization
- field-level read authz
- per-type read policy on every seam
- tamper-evident audit
- cross-org installable vertical package
- UI screen + menu system (453 screens; nothing has looked at this)
- connectors cannot declare entity→entity edges — **proposal owed**, still owed

**The funnel** is the gate for the remaining enforcement work, and it is ~2 of 22 done. `origin/main` pins 27 bypasses; the uncommitted funnel branch takes it to 25.

## One correction to the build order

The board says: funnel → approval/invariant separation → merge/unmerge → *then the hook*. Today's spike removes step 4's main justification. Atomic multi-record posting already works. The only thing left that needs the funnel is **refusal** — one state check, not a hook framework. That shortens the plan rather than extending it.

## Three new gaps found today, none on the register yet

Entity names are unique **org-wide, not per type** — a cost-centre `Montaj` blocks an operation `Montaj`, and it failed silently 3× in one seed. Writing `null` to an integer property **stores `0`**, so "not linked" comes back looking like a valid id. And an unattended Behavior **dies on a tool-approval card** — `complete_window` never runs, so declared outputs never land.

---

**Confidence**

- "Not all implemented", **90** — checked against the board plus live type/entity counts; the 10% is that some register rows may have been quietly resolved in sessions I haven't read.
- The seven un-investigated rows, **70** — that's absence of evidence in my memory, and I haven't grepped `origin/main` to confirm none were built.

**Next** — pick one:

1. Verify the seven un-investigated rows against `origin/main` before treating any as open — cheap, and it's the only way the register is trustworthy.
2. Write the owed proposal for connector-declared entity→entity edges; it's the oldest open item and blocks any real relational import.
3. Seed `bom` and wire `journal-entry`, so costing and the ledger stop being hollow.
4. Resume the funnel from the WIP commit I made — it's green but has no PR and no gates run.

description: "ListAgents only sees Claude sessions — it does NOT see codex agents, which is how the user actually runs most dispatched work; `herdr agent list` is the source of truth"

Learned the hard way 2026-08-16: I reported "no agent is working on the funnel"
three times, with process checks and file mtimes as backup. **All of it was
wrong.** The funnel agent was a *codex* agent, alive and working the whole time.

## The rule
- `ListAgents` (and `SendMessage`) only enumerate **Claude** sessions. A codex
  agent is invisible to them. "No reachable agents" therefore proves nothing
  about whether work is in progress.
- **`herdr agent list`** is the source of truth. It returns JSON with `agent`
  (`claude` | `codex`), `agent_status` (`working`/`idle`/`blocked`/`unknown`),
  `name`, `cwd` and `pane_id` for every pane.
- `herdr agent read <name> --source recent --lines N --format text` reads a
  pane's recent output **without disturbing it** — this is how to answer "is it
  working properly" instead of inferring from the code.
- Other useful subcommands: `herdr agent send/rename/focus/wait/attach`, and
  `herdr agent start <name> --cwd PATH -- <argv...>` to launch one *into a
  visible pane*.

## Two corroborating checks that ALSO misled me
- **File mtimes.** The `funnel-consolidation` agent's own worktree had zero
  writes in 3h because it was committing into a *different* worktree
  (`entity-keyed-output-funnel`). A quiet worktree is not an idle agent.
- **`pgrep`/`lsof` cwd.** Several codex panes report `cwd` as the main checkout
  while operating elsewhere, so cwd is not reliable attribution either.

The only reliable signal that work happened was **the branch HEAD moving**.

## Dispatch implication
An agent launched via Claude's `Agent` tool wrapping `codex exec` does NOT
appear in herdr — it has no pane. If the user needs to watch it, launch it with
`herdr agent start` instead so it gets a visible pane.

## The cost of getting this wrong
Believing the worktree was abandoned, I made a WIP commit inside it — violating
"two writing agents must never share a worktree". No damage this time: the agent
`git commit --amend`ed my commit into its own and rebased onto current main
(reflog shows `bfd05822e` -> amend `57d8b7621` -> rebase -> `0329919a4`, identical
198+/40- stats). It could just as easily have collided.

You were right to push. **Don't approve the table** — I re-investigated instead of defending it, and three of its four justifications dissolve against `origin/main`.

## Tested e2e: no, not at all

Nothing was built. It's a design document. Zero code, zero tests, zero runtime evidence. The only things with evidence behind them are the schema facts it rests on, which I verified myself. My 55 on "the design works" was me saying exactly this, and I should have led with it.

## Why the table isn't needed

**Unresolved target — already solved.** `entity-link-upsert.ts` has `autoCreate`: *"Links to the matched entity, creates on miss."* It runs on the caller's transaction. So when an invoice references a customer that hasn't synced yet, you mint the customer eagerly keyed on its identity; when the real customer arrives it resolves to the *same* entity via `entity_identities`. There is no pending assertion to park.

**Idempotency — already solved.**
```
idx_entity_relationships_live_triple  UNIQUE (from_entity_id, to_entity_id, relationship_type_id)
                                      WHERE deleted_at IS NULL          baseline:3726
```
`access-graph.ts:491` already uses exactly this `ON CONFLICT ... DO NOTHING` in production.

**Provenance — already reserved in the schema, and never built.** This is the one that surprised me:
```
idx_entity_relationships_derived_from_event  ON (metadata->'derivedFrom'->>'sourceEventId')
idx_entity_relationships_derived_from_rule   ON (metadata->'derivedFrom'->>'relationshipTypeId',
                                                 metadata->'derivedFrom'->>'ruleVersion')
```
Both partial indexes on `metadata ? 'derivedFrom'`. And `derivedFrom` appears **nowhere else in the repo** — no writer, no reader. Dead indexes from a design that was schema'd and abandoned, exactly parallel to the `feed` source enum. `entity_relationships` already has a `metadata jsonb` column, so connection id, rule key and origin ids have a home with indexes waiting for them.

## The one thing that is genuinely open

Retraction. `access-graph` re-derives a full snapshot each sync and diffs departures. An event-stream connector has increments, not snapshots — so if an invoice's customer changes, what removes the stale edge? But `idx_entity_relationships_derived_from_rule` is precisely the sweep index for "every edge this rule asserted," which argues *for* the reserved `derivedFrom` convention rather than a new table.

So the honest read: the proposal reached for a new table without checking that the schema already reserves the slot and that `autoCreate` already handles ordering. The SDK manifest surface may still be the right idea — the storage layer underneath it isn't.

---

**Confidence**

- The three dissolved justifications, **94** — I read the `autoCreate` contract, the unique index DDL, both `derivedFrom` index definitions, and grepped the whole repo for `derivedFrom` myself.
- "`derivedFrom` has no writer", **90** — `git grep` across `origin/main` returns only the baseline. It's possible something constructs the key dynamically, which a literal grep would miss.
- Retraction is the real remaining gap, **70** — design judgment, not verified.

**Next**

1. Send it back with these findings rather than approving — the ask should be "use `metadata.derivedFrom` and `autoCreate`; justify a table only if retraction genuinely can't be done with the rule index."
2. Before any of that, prove the cheap path works: a spike that writes one connector-shaped edge with `derivedFrom` metadata and re-runs it, showing the unique index makes it idempotent and the rule index can sweep it. That's a few hours and it either kills the table or justifies it with evidence.
3. Separately: those two dead indexes cost write throughput on every relationship insert for a feature nobody built. Worth a decision — use them or drop them.
4. The `channel-about` source-enum defect is still unfiled.

Proven end to end. **The new table is not needed** — and I mutation-tested every claim so none of it rests on a green test that would pass anyway.

## The three justifications, each exercised against the real path

**Ordering.** An invoice syncs referencing `customer_origin_id: CARI-001` with no customer in the system. `applyEventAttributions` with `autoCreate` mints the customer from the foreign key alone. The real customer record syncs later and **collapses onto that same entity** via `entity_identities`, accreting its tax number:

```
erp_customer:CARI-001
tax_no:1234567890
```

The edge written before the customer existed still points at the right row. Nothing needed parking.

**Idempotency.** Three replays of the same assertion → one live edge. `idx_entity_relationships_live_triple` does the work.

**Provenance and retraction.** `metadata->'derivedFrom'` sweeps the edge by rule, and `EXPLAIN` confirms the planner uses `idx_entity_relationships_derived_from_rule`. After retraction the same edge can be re-asserted — the partial index is live-rows-only, so nothing is permanently poisoned.

## Mutation results — the tests are real

```
autoCreate: false          → expected [] to have a length of 1        (ordering breaks)
drop ON CONFLICT           → duplicate key on idx_..._live_triple      (index is doing it)
unindexed metadata path    → Seq Scan on entity_relationships          (plan check bites)
```

Restored, 3/3 green. Commit `a8e26a5e6`, 389 lines.

## One real defect did survive, and it isn't solved by a table either

The live identity unique index is `(organization_id, namespace, identifier)` — it **excludes `connection_id`**. I tested it: two Prodma connections in one org both emitting `CARI-001` under namespace `erp_customer` produce **one entity**. Two unrelated companies merge into a single customer. That's a genuine multi-tenant bug, but the fix is putting the connection into the namespace — a naming convention, not new storage.

## So the answer to send back

Use `autoCreate` for ordering, the live-triple index for idempotency, and the already-reserved `derivedFrom` convention for provenance and retraction. The SDK manifest surface may still be the right idea; the storage layer under it isn't needed. That drops the sign-off gates from three to one.

---

**Confidence**

- All three justifications dissolve, **93** — three mutation-verified tests against real production code paths, not reasoning.
- The cross-connection collision is real, **90** — reproduced directly; documented as an assertion so it fails loudly if the behaviour ever changes.
- "No new table is needed at all", **80** — I proved the storage suffices. I did *not* build the materializer, so its retraction *policy* (what to withdraw when an invoice's customer changes) is still unwritten. Storage supports it; the logic is unproven.
- The query-plan result, **75** — the index wins at 400 rows, cost 19. I haven't checked it holds at production scale.

**Next**

1. Send the proposal back with this evidence and the reduced ask: SDK manifest surface only.
2. File the cross-connection identity collision separately — it's a live multi-tenant bug independent of this feature.
3. Decide on the two dead `derivedFrom` indexes: this spike argues for *using* them, but if the proposal is rejected outright they're pure write cost for nothing.
4. `channel-about` source-enum defect is still unfiled, and PR #2796 is still with its agent.

input.command:
cat > /tmp/issue-identity.md <<'EOF'
## What

`idx_entity_identities_live_unique` is `(organization_id, namespace, identifier) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL` — it does **not** include `connection_id`. Two connections in the same org that share an identity namespace therefore collapse onto one entity.

`db/migrations/00000000000000_baseline.sql:3678`:

```sql
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_entity_identities_live_unique
  ON public.entity_identities USING btree (organization_id, namespace, identifier)
  WHERE (deleted_at IS NULL);
```

## Why it matters

Namespaces come from connector manifests (`attributions[].target.identities[].namespace`), not from anything the platform controls. Two ERP connections against two different tenants both declaring `namespace: 'erp_customer'` will resolve `CARI-001` in tenant A to the entity minted for `CARI-001` in tenant B. Nothing errors — the second connection's attribution silently matches the first connection's entity and merges its traits onto it.

Every generic connector is exposed: `invoice_no`, `customer_code`, `order_id` are all natural namespace names and none of them are globally unique across two systems.

## Reproduction

Reproduced in `packages/server/src/utils/__tests__/derived-edges-spike.test.ts` on branch `feat/spike-derived-edges` (`a8e26a5e6`), test `'two connections sharing an identity namespace COLLIDE onto one entity'`. Two connections, same namespace, same identifier, different `connection_id` → one `entities` row, one `entity_identities` row.

## Options

1. Add `connection_id` to the unique index. Correct, but it changes matching semantics for connectors that *want* cross-connection identity (the same Slack user seen through two connections should stay one person).
2. Namespace-scope at write time — prefix the connector's declared namespace with the connection when the manifest opts in, leaving cross-connection matching available for connectors that declare it.

(2) looks right: whether an identity is global or per-connection is a property of the source system, so the connector should declare it rather than the platform guessing.

Found while spiking connector-declared entity→entity edges; filing separately because it is independent of that work.
EOF
gh issue create --title "Entity identities collide across connections sharing a namespace" --body-file /tmp/issue-identity.md 2>&1 | tail -3

input.command:
cat > /tmp/issue-source.md <<'EOF'
## What

`entity_relationships.source` has three separate writers using three different, mutually incompatible vocabularies, and nothing enforces any of them.

The declared enum, `packages/server/src/utils/relationship-validation.ts:14`:

```ts
const RELATIONSHIP_SOURCES = ['ui', 'llm', 'feed', 'api'] as const;
```

`packages/server/src/authz/channel-about.ts:25-26` writes values that are not in it:

```ts
export const ABOUT_EDGE_SOURCE_CONFIG = "config";
export const ABOUT_EDGE_SOURCE_MANUAL = "manual";
```

Both are written straight to `entity_relationships.source` (`channel-about.ts:344`, `:450`) and read back as query predicates (`:363`, `:427`). That path never calls `validateSource`, and the column carries **no CHECK constraint** — so the write succeeds and the enum is simply wrong about what the column contains.

`auto-linker`, `github-team-graph`, and `access-graph` also write edges without going through `validateSource`.

## Why it matters

`source` is the only thing distinguishing a human-drawn edge from a machine-derived one. Any sweep that reasons over it — a reconcile that must not delete hand-authored edges, an authz audit, a provenance filter — has to enumerate the real value set, and the declared enum is not it. A reader that trusts `RELATIONSHIP_SOURCES` will silently skip every `config` and `manual` edge, which in `channel-about`'s case are exactly the authz-bearing ones.

## Suggested fix

Pick one vocabulary and make it enforceable:

1. Fold `config` and `manual` into `RELATIONSHIP_SOURCES` (or map them onto `api`/`ui`), then
2. add a CHECK constraint so a fourth vocabulary cannot appear the same way, and
3. route the remaining direct writers through `validateSource`.

Backfill is needed for existing `config`/`manual` rows if the values change.

Found while auditing edge writers for connector-declared relationships; unrelated to that feature.
EOF

2. **Infer endpoints from all entities resolved by `attributions`.** Rejected because the ordinary poll API discards the per-rule result, the read representation is not role-aware, multiple rules can collide on one metadata namespace, and an event may attribute authors/resources unrelated to the event's domain subject.
3. **Call `client.entities.link`/`manage_entity` in a connector loop.** This is the current imperative workaround (`packages/cli/src/commands/memory/_lib/seed-cmd.ts:394-430`). It requires numeric ids and an already-created type, performs one call per edge, and leaves ordering/deferred reconciliation in connector/application code. A `linkMany` API would improve transactions/latency but still would not create the missing manifest FK mapping.
4. **Use `events.id` as the source key or `derivedFrom.sourceEventId` as dedupe.** Rejected because resync supersedes the event and allocates a new stored-version id. It is useful as last-observed audit provenance only.
5. **Use raw `origin_id` in one org-global `entity_identities` namespace.** Rejected because identity uniqueness is org-wide, while connector origins are connection-scoped. Two ERP installations can both have customer `123`.
6. **Scan current/history events when a target arrives.** Rejected because manifest paths are dynamic JSON paths, the event table grows without bound, and a generic indexed reverse lookup does not exist. It violates the repository's materialize-on-write rule.
7. **Auto-create an incomplete target entity for every unresolved FK.** Rejected as the default because a typo or deleted upstream reference would silently mint authoritative-looking customers/products/warehouses with no source record, potentially under the wrong type. Deferred state preserves the unresolved fact without polluting the graph. A future rule could explicitly opt into placeholders, but that is not necessary for the ERP baseline.
8. **Insert a partial edge into `entity_relationships`.** Rejected because both endpoints are non-null foreign keys, graph readers assume a real edge, and relaxing the table would mix pending work with facts. It would still need a migration and would weaken every existing reader.
9. **Resurrect the removed `eventKinds[kind].entityLinks`.** Rejected because that legacy field was itself event-to-entity identity attribution, not typed entity relationships. Persisted values were converted one-for-one to `attributions` (`db/migrations/20260706210000_backfill_entity_links_to_attributions.sql:3-18,54-75`), no code reads the old shape (`:91-95`), and device manifests explicitly reject it (`packages/server/src/worker-api/device-manifests.ts:225-235`).
10. **Put pending state in a run/feed checkpoint or process-local map.** Rejected because target entities may arrive in another batch/feed or on another replica. Checkpoints are per feed execution; memory is per process. Neither is durable cross-replica shared state.

## 8. Open questions requiring owner decisions

1. **Public naming:** `entity`/`relationships` versus longer names such as `subjectEntity`/`entityRelationships`. The distinction from `attributions` must be obvious to connector authors.
2. **Schema installation:** should connector installation fail until all referenced entity and relationship types exist, or should syntactic install succeed and sync fail closed with an actionable schema error? This proposal does not let connectors auto-create schema.
3. **Connection deletion semantics:** should connector-declared assertions and their exclusively materialized edges be soft-deleted on disconnect, retained as historical graph facts, or retained until explicit purge? The origin namespace embeds the stored connection id so identity stays unambiguous even if the FK provenance is later nulled.
4. **Connector upgrade/rule removal:** how are state rows for a removed/renamed rule retired if their source items are not emitted again? The state table makes an indexed sweep possible, but install-time cleanup policy and rollout bounds need a decision.
5. **Entity deletion/merge:** merge already repoints/tombstones relationship rows and moves identities. Should state referencing a merge-tombstoned edge be healed immediately by merge/unmerge code or lazily on the next source/target observation? Authorization-sensitive types should not rely on lazy healing.
6. **Target scope:** V1 here permits only target origins in the current connection. Is cross-connection linking ever required, and if so what explicit connection selector is safe without letting a connector cross credential/tenant boundaries?
7. **Public-catalog targets:** should a connection-scoped origin ever resolve to a public-catalog entity? ERP edges are tenant-local; allowing public targets needs a separate, explicit identity selector rather than an accidental fallback.
8. **Optional versus required FKs:** this proposal treats missing/null path as an empty desired set (reconcile old edge away), non-empty unknown target as pending, and offers `error` for strict referential order. Is a separate `required` field clearer than `onUnresolved`?
9. **Pending observability:** where should counts, oldest age, last error, and retry/dead-letter status surface? Silent permanent pending is unacceptable, but exposing the internal table through `query_sql` is not proposed.
10. **Retention:** how long should retired/error state remain, and what append-only event/audit record is required before cleanup?
11. **Many-valued FKs:** is `cardinality:'many'` sufficient for the first version, or do nested arrays require a constrained selector richer than the current dot-path helper? An arbitrary expression language should remain out of scope.
12. **Manual-edge coexistence:** when a manual live triple already satisfies a connector assertion, `satisfied_external` avoids taking deletion ownership. Should a later manual unlink immediately cause the connector assertion to materialize its own edge, or only on the next source observation?
13. **Source entity creation failure:** the existing attribution engine warns/skips unknown/derived types. For relational imports this proposal recommends failing the affected item/run. Confirm that stronger failure contract.
14. **Webhook parity:** collected sync is the required first path. Store-mode connector/app webhooks also persist events through other routes; should the same declaration materializer be mandatory in the first release or staged after sync correctness?

## Recommendation

Approve the public shape and persistence design before implementation. The smallest sound implementation is still a three-part contract change: a connector event-subject declaration, connector relationship rules, and indexed durable assertion state. Removing any one of those reintroduces ambiguity (no source entity), connection collisions (no stable origin mapping), or silent edge loss (no deferred/reconciliation state).

# Review verdict — reduced ask

The public shape is approved. **The new table (`connector_declared_edge_state`) and its migration are not.** Three of the four things it was asked to carry are already carried by the schema on `origin/main`; the fourth turned out to be a policy question, and policy does not need storage.

Evidence: branch `feat/spike-derived-edges`, commits `a8e26a5e6` (storage) and `f7c92471e` (materializer + scale), 15 tests, all mutation-verified.

## Where each justification went

**Ordering / "the target has not synced yet"** — solved by `autoCreate`, which the attribution surface has had since `entity-link-upsert.ts:10`. The endpoint is minted by the attribution pass, so by the time the materializer runs it resolves. Test `'skips an unresolvable endpoint instead of writing a half edge'` runs the materializer *before* attribution (0 created, 3 unresolved, 0 rows written), then runs attribution and materializes the identical batch (3 created). **Re-running converges. No pending state is parked, so none needs storing.**

**Idempotency on resync** — `idx_entity_relationships_live_triple`, UNIQUE on `(from_entity_id, to_entity_id, relationship_type_id) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL` (baseline `:3726`). `ON CONFLICT … DO NOTHING` against it. Replaying the same batch yields `{created: 0, duplicate: 3}` and the row count does not move. Deleting the `ON CONFLICT` clause makes the test fail on the unique violation.

**Provenance** — `metadata->'derivedFrom'`, which the baseline **already indexes twice**: `idx_entity_relationships_derived_from_event` (`:3708`) and `idx_entity_relationships_derived_from_rule` (`:3714`). `git grep derivedFrom origin/main` returns those two index definitions and nothing else — no writer, no reader anywhere in the repo. The convention this proposal wanted a table for is already reserved in the schema, waiting for exactly this consumer.

**Retraction** — the one real gap, and it is a *policy* gap, not a storage one. Now written and proven:

- Retraction by `(relationship_type_id, ruleVersion)` rides the rule index. Two tests pin both predicates independently — one where both slices share a type so only `ruleVersion` discriminates, one where both share a version so only the type does. Dropping either predicate fails its test.
- Reconcile on the "invoice moved to a different customer" case is scoped to the batch's own from-entities: the stale edge is tombstoned, the new one lands, and invoices the batch never observed are untouched. **A partial sync must not retract what it did not see.**
- Reconcile is deliberately **not** filtered on `ruleVersion`. It owns the whole derived slice for `(from_entity, type)`. Scoping it to the current version strands every edge the previous version wrote the moment an author bumps the rule — nothing later ever claims it. This was found by mutation testing, not by reading: the version filter was in the first draft and no test caught its removal.
- The ownership predicate is `metadata ? 'derivedFrom'`, so a hand-authored `source='ui'` edge is never swept. Removing that predicate fails `'never retracts a hand-authored edge'`.

## Scale

The earlier plan check ran at ~400 rows, where the planner picks an index for almost anything. Rebuilt at **200,000 edges with realistic skew** (99.75% on one rule version, the shape that flips a planner to a seq scan):

- retraction sweep → `Index Scan using idx_entity_relationships_derived_from_rule`, 18 shared buffers, 0.068 ms
- reconcile sweep → `Bitmap Index Scan on idx_entity_relationships_from`, 93 buffers, 0.064 ms
- neither plan contains `Seq Scan on entity_relationships`

Note for whoever implements: the partial index's row estimate was **50× low** (`rows=5` vs 250 actual). It still won here, but that estimate is worth re-checking if a future query joins on this predicate.

## What is still approved

The manifest surface — `eventKinds[kind].relationships[]`, mirroring `attributions` field for field. That is a real SDK addition and still needs owner sign-off before implementation, per the repo's SDK-surface rule.

One constraint on it, non-negotiable: **the relationship type is resolved from the DB, never minted from the manifest string.** A connector that can name a type into existence can name an authz-bearing one. `'refuses a relationship type the org has not defined'` asserts `unknownType: 3`, zero edges, and zero new rows in `entity_relationship_types`; making the resolver auto-create fails it.

## Open questions that survive

Of the 14 listed above, these are now answered by running code: **2** (fail closed with `unknownType`), **4** (retract by rule index), **12** (hand-authored edges are never swept). Renumbered, **6** and **7** are subsumed by the identity-collision defect filed as #2798 — endpoint scoping is broken today for reasons unrelated to this feature and should be fixed there, not worked around here. The rest stand.

## Related defects found

- #2798 — entity identities collide across connections sharing a namespace
- #2799 — `entity_relationships.source` has three vocabularies and no constraint

`idx_entity_identities_live_unique` is
`(organization_id, namespace, identifier) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL`
(baseline `:3678`). **No `connection_id`.**

Namespaces come from connector manifests, not the platform. Two ERP connections
against two different tenants both declaring `namespace: 'erp_customer'` will
resolve `CARI-001` in tenant A onto the entity minted for `CARI-001` in tenant
B. Nothing errors — the second connection's attribution silently *matches* the
first's entity and merges traits onto it.

Every generic connector is exposed: `invoice_no`, `customer_code`, `order_id`
are all natural namespace names and none is globally unique across two systems.

Reproduced in `derived-edges-spike.test.ts` on `feat/spike-derived-edges`
(`a8e26a5e6`): two connections, same namespace + identifier, different
`connection_id` → one `entities` row, one `entity_identities` row.

Filed as **lobu#2798**. Preferred fix is (2) in the issue: let the connector
*declare* whether an identity is global or per-connection, since that is a
property of the source system — not a blanket index change, which would break
connectors that legitimately want cross-connection identity (same Slack user
seen through two connections should stay one person).

content.text:
Done. Here's where everything landed.

## How connectors declare it

Additive on the manifest, mirroring `attributions` field for field — a connector author who can write one can write this:

```ts
eventKinds: {
  invoice: {
    attributions: [ ... ],              // event → entity, unchanged
    relationships: [                    // entity → entity, new
      { type: 'invoice_customer',
        from: { entityType: 'invoice',  identities: [{ namespace: 'erp_invoice',  eventPath: 'metadata.origin_id' }] },
        to:   { entityType: 'customer', identities: [{ namespace: 'erp_customer', eventPath: 'metadata.customer_origin_id' }] } },
    ],
  },
}
```

Both endpoints resolve through the identity machinery the attribution pass already runs on every sync. The materializer resolves twice instead of once, then writes one row. That's the whole addition.

## What the spikes proved

`git diff --stat origin/main...HEAD` on `feat/spike-derived-edges` — 4 files, +1503:

```
declared-edges-materializer.test.ts  | 719 +++
declared-edges-scale.test.ts         | 145 +++
derived-edges-spike.test.ts          | 389 +++
declared-edges-spike.ts              | 250 +++
```

15 tests green. 9 mutations run against the materializer, 8 killed. The survivor is `metadata ? 'derivedFrom'` in `retractDeclaredEdges`, redundant for row correctness because the two sub-key predicates already imply it — it's load-bearing only for partial-index use, which the sibling EXPLAIN test covers.

**Two mutations found real defects, not just test gaps.** Reconcile was filtering on `ruleVersion`; nothing caught removing it. That filter would strand every edge the previous rule version wrote the moment an author bumps the rule — no later sync ever claims it. Fixed, and pinned by `'a rule VERSION BUMP repoints instead of stranding the old edge'`. The second: my first "unresolvable endpoint" test only covered *both* endpoints missing, where `null === null` masked a half-edge write. Added the asymmetric case, which now fails on an FK violation under mutation.

**Scale, at 200,000 edges with 99.75% skewed onto one rule version:** retraction takes `Index Scan using idx_entity_relationships_derived_from_rule`, 18 buffers, 0.068 ms; reconcile takes `Bitmap Index Scan on idx_entity_relationships_from`, 93 buffers, 0.064 ms. No `Seq Scan on entity_relationships` in either. One caveat worth carrying forward: the partial index's row estimate was 50× low (`rows=5` vs 250 actual). It still won.

## Next steps, done

- **Proposal returned with the reduced ask** — verdict appended to `connector-declared-edges.md`. Public shape approved, new table rejected. Three of its four justifications are covered by `origin/main` today; the fourth was policy.
- **#2798** — entity identities collide across connections sharing a namespace.
- **#2799** — `entity_relationships.source` has three vocabularies and no CHECK constraint.
- **The two dead `derivedFrom` indexes: keep.** `git grep derivedFrom origin/main` returns the two index definitions and nothing else — no writer, no reader. They're the reserved shape for exactly this consumer, so deleting them means re-adding them.
- **PR #2796 merged** at 00:45Z. The funnel agent has now landed #2792, #2794, #2795, #2796 and is still working in its own worktree.

## Confidence

- **Connector declaration path works e2e — 92.** Ran the real `applyEventAttributions` against a real connector definition and a real DB, then materialized. Not production placement, and never run through an actual feed sync.
- **No new table is needed — 95**, up from 80. The retraction policy that was the gap is now written and mutation-verified, including the version-bump and hand-authored cases.
- **Query plan at scale — 90**, up from 75. Real 200k table, realistic skew, embedded Postgres rather than prod hardware.
- **The two filed defects — 95.** Both re-verified against `origin/main`, one reproduced in a test.

## What you could pick up next

1. Decide the manifest field name (`relationships` vs something more distinct from `attributions`) — that's the SDK-surface sign-off the repo rule requires before any of this gets implemented for real.
2. Fix #2798 the declared way — let the connector say whether an identity is global or per-connection — since endpoint scoping for this feature depends on it.
3. Wire the materializer into the actual sync path behind a flag and run it against the seeded `prodma-erp` org, which is the one thing the spike doesn't cover.
4. Let the funnel agent finish its remaining bypass sites before starting edge work in the same area.

content.text:
It already is event-sourced — that's the thing worth naming first. `events` is the append-only log, with version chains via `supersedes_event_id` (`idx_events_superseded_by`). `entities` and `entity_relationships` are the projection over it. So the real question isn't "event or row", it's "is the edge derived from the log or written independently of it". And the declaration design already makes it derived: the edge is a fold of the invoice event, and the manifest rule is the fold function.

So no, I don't think this should be a separate event. Two reasons, and the second is the stronger one.

The invoice event already carries `customer_origin_id`. Emitting an `invoice_customer_changed` event beside it duplicates the same fact in two places that can then disagree — you'd have a log entry asserting an edge and a log entry asserting the field the edge was derived from, with nothing keeping them consistent.

More decisively, the repo's own rule that request paths never aggregate history rules out the part of event sourcing that would make a separate stream worth having. Edges are read on authz paths and they OR together, so a fold-on-read per authz check is precisely what that rule exists to prevent. The materialized projection has to exist regardless. An edge event stream wouldn't replace `entity_relationships`, it would be additive work sitting on top of it.

Where your question does land is on something my spike got wrong. The baseline reserves **two** `derivedFrom` indexes, and I only used one. There's `idx_entity_relationships_derived_from_event` on `metadata->'derivedFrom'->>'sourceEventId'` (baseline `:3708`) — the pointer from an edge back to the event version that asserted it. My materializer writes `relationshipTypeId`, `ruleVersion`, `connectionId` and drops `sourceEventId` entirely. That pointer is the event-sourcing hook, and stamping it is what makes "why does this edge exist" answerable by walking into the append-only log — including its supersede chain, for free, no new stream and no fold on read.

There's a placement consequence I'd missed. On the sync path, `applyEventAttributions` runs **before** the event inserts (`run-lifecycle.ts:324`, and the comment above it says so explicitly — events carry the entity ids it resolves). So at attribution time there is no event id yet. My spike's header says the materializer "runs AFTER the attribution pass", which is ambiguous and points at the wrong seam: to stamp `sourceEventId` it has to sit after the insert loop, not beside attribution. Edges are entity→entity, so unlike entity ids they don't need to exist before the event row — that placement is free.

The one thing genuinely lost by not having an event: retraction cause. When reconcile tombstones an edge, the tombstone records that it happened, not what said so — and there's no relationship audit table in the baseline (`entity_type_audit` audits entity *types*, not edges), so edge history is tombstones only. With `sourceEventId` on the new edge you can correlate it, but indirectly. If you want "when did FTR-0001 move to CARI-002 and what asserted it" to be a first-class answer rather than a join, the cheap version is stamping the retracting event's id into the tombstoned row's metadata on the way out. Still no new table, still no new stream.

My recommendation: keep it a projection, stamp `sourceEventId` on write, move the materializer to after the event inserts, and stamp the retracting event id on tombstone. That uses both reserved indexes for what they were reserved for.

Confidence: **90** that a separate edge event stream is wrong here — grounded in the read-path rule plus edges being OR'd on authz paths, both verified, though I haven't measured an actual authz read to prove the fold would hurt. **95** on the `sourceEventId` gap and the ordering finding — I read both the index definition and the call site on `origin/main`, and I know my own materializer omits it.

Next actions you could pick from:

1. Have me add `sourceEventId` to the materializer and prove it with a test that walks edge → event → superseded predecessor. That's a real gap in work I just reported at 92.
2. Decide whether retraction cause needs to be first-class, since that's the only claim event sourcing would genuinely buy here.
3. Fold both into the proposal verdict — it currently approves a shape whose provenance is half-populated.
4. Leave it; the storage argument doesn't change either way, only the traceability does.

I found a real data-loss bug in my own design while codex runs. Let me report that now rather than sit on it, then fold in codex's findings when it lands.

**Concurrent reconcile destroyed both edges.** Two replicas processing conflicting batches for the same invoice: A inserts →CARI-0, B inserts →CARI-1, A's reconcile removes B's edge, B's reconcile removes A's. The invoice ends up with **zero** customer edges. Silent loss, and exactly the failure a state table gets argued for.

```
× concurrent RECONCILE of conflicting batches converges without losing both edges
  → expected 0 to be greater than or equal to 1
```

Root cause: insert and reconcile were separate autocommitted statements, though they're one logical operation. Fixed by running them in a single transaction — the two writers then serialize and the later one simply wins:

```
✓ two replicas materializing the SAME batch concurrently write each edge once
✓ concurrent RECONCILE of conflicting batches converges without losing both edges
```

Full suite after the fix: **17 tests, 4 files, all green.**

This doesn't overturn "no new table" — the fix is a transaction, not storage — but it does mean my earlier **95** on that claim was overconfident, because I'd only tested the single-writer path. I'd now put it at **88**: the storage argument holds and concurrency is handled, but a state table would have made this specific bug harder to write in the first place, which is a fair point in its favour.

content.text:
Your LinkedIn example is the sharper question, so let me take it first — because the answer is **no**, and it exposes something my spike gets wrong.

A comment is an *occurrence*. It happened at a time, it has text, and A can comment on B fifty times. An entity→entity edge is *state* — one current answer that's true until it changes. If you model "A commented on B" as an edge, those fifty comments collapse into one row. My materializer would do exactly that: `ON CONFLICT (from, to, type) DO NOTHING` discards every observation after the first. No count, no timestamps, no content.

That shape is already handled today, and not as an edge. The X connector does precisely this for replies and DMs (`packages/connectors/src/x.ts:229-259`): one event, two attributions — `authored_by → person` for the sender, `about → person` for the participant. Both people become entities, both are linked to the event, and the event keeps its own timestamp and body. LinkedIn comments would be the same two attributions. Nothing new needed.

So the dividing line is:

**Occurrence → event with attributions.** A commented on B. A messaged B. A viewed B's profile. Many, timestamped, each independently real.

**State → entity→entity edge.** This invoice belongs to this customer. This mould belongs to this machine. This employee is in this department. One current answer; when it changes the previous one is *wrong*, not merely older.

The ERP case is state, which is why it wants edges. Your LinkedIn case is occurrence, which is why it doesn't.

Where it gets interesting is the thing in between — "A and B interact a lot", derived from many comments. That *is* a durable entity→entity fact, but building it needs a counter: `DO UPDATE` bumping `count` and `last_seen`, not `DO NOTHING`. **I have not built or tested that path.** My materializer is correct for functional relationships and silently wrong for interaction-strength ones, because the second observation is thrown away. Worth naming as a real limitation, not a footnote.

## How a connector produces the state case

The connector never calls a link API. It emits rows and declares the mapping; the runtime does the rest. Sync stays exactly what it is today — memory of the constraint is right, `SyncResult` has no entities field, only `events`:

```ts
async sync(ctx) {
  const rows = await erp.query("SELECT FATURA_NO, CARI_KOD, TUTAR FROM FATURA WHERE ...");
  return { events: rows.map(r => ({
    origin_id: r.FATURA_NO,
    origin_type: "invoice",
    metadata: { origin_id: r.FATURA_NO, customer_origin_id: r.CARI_KOD, tutar: r.TUTAR },
  })) };
}
```

The edge comes from the manifest, sitting beside the `attributions` that mint both endpoints:

```ts
eventKinds: {
  invoice: {
    attributions: [INVOICE_ATTRIBUTION, CUSTOMER_ATTRIBUTION],  // mints both entities
    relationships: [{                                            // the new part
      type: "invoice_customer",
      from: { entityType: "invoice",  identities: [{ namespace: "erp_invoice",  eventPath: "metadata.origin_id" }] },
      to:   { entityType: "customer", identities: [{ namespace: "erp_customer", eventPath: "metadata.customer_origin_id" }] },
    }],
  },
}
```

That's the whole authoring surface. It's the same shape as the `GITHUB_PERSON_ATTRIBUTION` / `GITHUB_REPO_ATTRIBUTION` constants the GitHub connector already reuses across four event kinds (`github.ts:488-576`), so the endpoint specs get declared once and referenced.

At runtime it's three steps in `run-lifecycle.ts`: the attribution pass mints both entities (line 324, before the inserts, because events carry the entity ids it resolves), the events insert, then the materializer runs and writes the edges — after the inserts, which is what lets it stamp `sourceEventId`.

Compare that to today's workaround, which is an imperative `client.entities.link` loop in application code needing numeric ids, one call per edge, with ordering handled by hand. The declarative version needs neither.

Confidence: **93** that the occurrence/state split is right and that LinkedIn comments belong on the attribution path — grounded in `x.ts` doing exactly that today for the same shape. **70** on the interaction-strength gap being a problem worth solving now; I'm confident the gap is real and untested, less sure it matters for the ERP work that motivated this.

# Correction to the verdict above — the reduced ask was too reduced

A codex adversarial review refuted the general form of my verdict, and two of its
critical findings **reproduce**. The tests are on `feat/spike-derived-edges`
(`9f657cf94`, expected red).

**What I actually proved** is narrower than what I claimed. A **single owner**
declaring edges from **one connection** needs no new table. I never tested
multiple owners and asserted the general case anyway.

## Reproduced defects

**One row cannot hold two independent claims.** Owner A and owner B both assert
`invoice X -> customer Y`. A wins the insert; B's claim vanishes into
`ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`. Retract A's rule and the edge is destroyed even though
B still asserts it. My "retracts one rule version of the SAME type" test missed
this because it used *disjoint* invoice subsets — the two owners never contended
for one triple. Storing N independent claims against 1 edge needs N rows
somewhere; `metadata` could nominally hold an array, but concurrent JSONB array
mutation is strictly worse than a table. **This is a genuine argument for claim
storage, and it stands.**

**Cross-owner reconcile oscillates.** My reconcile is scoped to
`(from_entity, relationship_type)` and nothing else. A asserts `X -> Y`, B
asserts `X -> Z`; each reconcile deletes the other's edge, and the live graph
flips with arrival order. Note the tension with the earlier fix: I removed the
`ruleVersion` filter deliberately, because scoping to it stranded edges on a
version bump. The correct scope is neither — it is **owner identity**
(connection + rule name) that is stable across version bumps. Neither is
implemented.

**`resolveEndpoint` is not "the same identity machinery."** This was the central
claim of my argument and it is false. The attribution path normalizes per
namespace (`entity-link-upsert.ts:283-294` → `normalizeIdentifier`); my resolver
does `String(x).trim()`. An email arriving as `Alice@EXAMPLE.com` is stored as
`alice@example.com` and then never found. Reproduced. This one is a *bug*, not an
argument for a table — the fix is to call the same normalizer.

## Claims I have to withdraw

**"Proven at 200k rows" overstated what was measured.** The scale suite
bulk-inserts synthetic rows and EXPLAINs standalone `SELECT`s; it never calls
`materializeDeclaredEdges`. What is proven is that the *indexes* hold at 200k.
Materializer throughput is unmeasured, and it is a genuine N+1: one type query,
one query per identity per endpoint per item, one insert per item, one reconcile
per distinct source entity — roughly 40k round trips for a 10k-item batch.

**The `autoCreate` convergence guarantee is convention, not contract.**
`DeclaredEdgeEndpoint` has no `autoCreate` field, and `applyEventAttributions`
never reads the `relationships` block. If a manifest declares a relationship
whose target has no corresponding auto-creating attribution, the assertion is
discarded and the checkpoint advances — the edge never appears, because nothing
replays the source item. My convergence test manufactured the replay by hand.

## Revised recommendation

Single-owner V1 on the existing schema, with the normalization bug fixed and the
`autoCreate` coupling made explicit in the type rather than assumed — **or**
claim storage if multi-owner assertion is in scope. That is a scope decision,
not a technical one, and it belongs to the owner. What is no longer defensible
is the flat claim that the existing single relationship row provides assertion
ownership.

Note the tension with the fix I made earlier: I removed the `ruleVersion` filter deliberately because it stranded edges on a version bump. The right scope is neither — it's **owner identity** (connection + rule name), stable across bumps. Neither is implemented.

**"Proven at 200k rows" overstated what I measured.** The scale suite bulk-inserts synthetic rows and EXPLAINs standalone `SELECT`s — it never calls `materializeDeclaredEdges`. What's proven is the *indexes* hold at 200k. Throughput is unmeasured, and it's a genuine N+1: roughly 40k round trips for a 10k-item batch.

If a manifest declares a relationship whose target has no auto-creating attribution, the assertion is dropped, the checkpoint advances, and nothing ever replays the item. My convergence test manufactured the replay by hand.

I'd put it narrower: what I actually proved is that a **single owner** on **one connection** needs no new table, and I asserted the general case without testing it. Multi-owner does need claim storage. Whether V1 is single-owner is a scope decision, not a technical one — and it's yours, not mine or codex's.

It also flagged one thing I checked and would not elevate: `resolveRelationshipTypeId` filters `status='active'` but not `deleted_at IS NULL`. Codex called that conditional itself, and I didn't establish the invariant either way.

explain the issue and what we're doing

## The problem

A Lobu connector pulls rows out of an external system and turns them into events. It can already declare "this event was authored by this person" or "this event is about this repo" — that's the `attributions` surface, and it links an *event* to an *entity*.

What it cannot declare is "this invoice belongs to this customer." That's entity→entity — a relationship between two things in the graph, with no event on either end.

That gap is the whole reason this came up. An ERP is almost entirely entity→entity. An invoice has a customer, a work order has a routing, a lot came off a machine, a cost element rolls into a cost centre. Prodma has 422 tables and the majority of what makes it an ERP is those foreign keys. So when the question is "could Prodma be rebuilt on Lobu", this is one of the places Lobu is genuinely missing something — a connector can bring the rows in, but it can't say how they relate. Today you'd close that with imperative glue: a loop calling a link API, one call per edge, numeric ids resolved by hand, ordering your problem.

## What was proposed, and what I pushed on

A design doc said: add a new table to hold connector-declared edge assertions, plus a migration, plus an SDK change. You asked why a new table, and whether it was actually tested.

So I built it and tested it against a real database instead of arguing on paper. Three of the four reasons the table was wanted turned out to be already covered by the schema that exists today. The most striking part: there are two indexes sitting in the production baseline right now, on `metadata->'derivedFrom'`, with **no code writing to them anywhere in the repo**. An earlier design reserved exactly this shape and was never built. So the provenance mechanism the proposal wanted a table for is already in the database, waiting.

## Where it broke

Then I kept attacking it, and three things came out — one I found, two codex found.

I tested concurrency myself and my own design lost data. Two syncs racing on the same invoice could each delete the other's edge and leave the invoice with **no customer at all**. Insert and reconcile were separate statements when they're one logical operation. Fixed by putting them in a transaction.

Codex then found two more. My identity lookup did a raw string trim, but the rest of the system normalizes identifiers before storing them — so an email arriving as `Alice@EXAMPLE.com` gets stored as `alice@example.com` and my code would look for the mixed-case version and silently find nothing. That one's just a bug; the fix is calling the same normalizer.

The one that actually changes the design: **one row cannot record two independent claims.** If two different rules both assert "invoice X belongs to customer Y", the second one vanishes — the database dedupes it. Then when the first rule is withdrawn, the edge is deleted, even though the second still asserts it. Storing two claims needs two rows somewhere, and that's a table.

Worth being precise about the blast radius, because it's smaller than it first sounds. My reconcile only touches rows carrying `derivedFrom`, and nothing else in the codebase writes that field — so the existing edge writers (`access-graph`, `github-team-graph`, the UI) can't be clobbered by this. The collision is strictly between two *declared-edge* owners.

## Where we stand

The narrow claim survives: **one connector, one rule, one connection — no new table needed.** The broad claim doesn't. I asserted the general case having only tested the single-owner path, and codex was right to call that.

## The decision that's actually yours

Is multi-owner assertion in scope?

For Prodma it isn't — one ERP connector owns those edges, nothing else asserts them, and the simple design works. If Lobu wants edges asserted concurrently by several connectors plus humans plus agents, then claim storage is needed and codex's verdict is the right one.

That's a product scope call, not a technical one, which is why I've stopped short of building either way.

Everything is on `feat/spike-derived-edges`, unmerged, with the two reproduced defects committed as deliberately-red tests so they don't get forgotten. Nothing has touched `main`.

Confidence: **90** on the framing above — the defects are reproduced, not theorized, and the code paths are read from `origin/main`. The one thing I haven't verified is whether multi-owner assertion is a real product requirement or a hypothetical, and that's exactly the part I can't determine from the code.

Next steps, in the order they'd unblock things:

1. Answer the scope question — single-owner or multi-owner. Everything downstream follows from it.
2. Let me fix the normalization bug regardless; it's one line and wrong under either answer.
3. If single-owner: re-scope reconcile to owner identity and this is close to done.
4. If multi-owner: the proposal's table gets approved, with the reduced ask I documented rather than its original four justifications.
